meta.blurb: Noor planned a healthy dinner, and by ten o'clock she was eating biscuits. Her uncle Idris, a retired dietitian, never blames her. He explains old hunger signals, clever food and busy lives, and helps her try small, kind changes.
meta.bible: Noor: a woman in her thirties who works in an office and wants to eat better, the main character. Idris: her uncle, a retired Dietitian with forty years of experience, patient and warm. Setting: Noor's small flat, a kitchen, a local market and a supermarket in a city. Key terms: Appetite, Ghrelin, Leptin, Hormones, Fibre, Protein, Ultra-processed, Cravings, Snacks, Biscuit, Habit, Willpower, Portion, Sleep, Stress, Dietitian, Supermarket, Lentils, Porridge, Oats, Calories, Cues. Voice: kind, clear and practical, never shaming; each beat explains one idea about why healthy eating feels hard and what helps. The science is real and hedged where it is uncertain: no invented numbers, studies or quotes. Hana: Noor's friendly colleague at the office, who keeps a jar of sweets on her desk and becomes her walking partner. Mrs Farah: a cheerful stallholder at the Saturday market who sells lentils, onions and greens. Sami: Noor's younger brother, a busy father who cooks for his small daughter Yara. Auntie Leila: Noor's generous aunt, who shows love by feeding people. Places: Mill Street with its bakery, the park Noor walks through on her way home, the Saturday market, the supermarket on Station Road. Things: the small green notebook in which Noor writes when the wanting comes; the Tired Evening Plan card on her fridge; the calendar with gold stars. Extra terms: Dopamine, Raisin, Lentil, Protein, Cortisol, Habit, Craving, Treats. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

beats.scene: Noor stands at an open fridge at night, looking toward a biscuit tin
beats.summary: Noor planned a healthy dinner but ends the night wanting biscuits, and wonders why eating well is so hard.

beats.scene: Noor at her office desk reads a list of old diet plans
beats.summary: The next morning Noor looks back at all the plans she has started and dropped this year.

beats.scene: Noor holds her phone to her ear in a corridor by a window
beats.summary: Noor phones her uncle Idris, a retired dietitian, and asks if he will help.

beats.scene: Idris at Noor's door holding oranges and a tin of tea
beats.summary: Idris arrives on Saturday with oranges and tea and lets Noor tell her story without interrupting.

beats.scene: Idris and Noor sit at a kitchen table with two cups of tea
beats.summary: Idris tells her that wanting biscuits is not a weakness; appetite is an old machine doing its job.

beats.scene: White-haired Idris holds a mug and talks in a warm kitchen
beats.summary: Idris tells Noor about forty years of dietitian work: most people already know what is healthy.

beats.scene: Noor shows Idris a shopping basket of vegetables she planned to cook
beats.summary: Noor protests that she knows what a healthy meal is, and Idris agrees that knowing is not the problem.

beats.scene: Idris holds up three fingers while Noor listens with her chin on her hand
beats.summary: Idris promises no scolding and no diet sheet, only curiosity about why, when and how she feels.

beats.scene: A small green notebook and a pencil lie on a wooden table
beats.summary: Idris gives Noor a small notebook, not to count food but to notice when the wanting comes.

beats.scene: Noor writes in the notebook at the kitchen counter beside an open biscuit tin
beats.summary: That evening Noor eats a biscuit, writes down the time and mood, and feels curious instead of ashamed.

beats.scene: Idris and Noor sit with tea and an old map
beats.summary: On his second visit Idris takes Noor back in time to a world where food was scarce.

beats.scene: Ancient people walk through dry grassland carrying baskets and sticks
beats.summary: For most of human history people searched for food for hours and could not be sure of finding it.

beats.scene: A group of people gather round a fire, eating roasted meat with fat dripping
beats.summary: Many scientists think bodies that sought rich, filling food and stored energy had an advantage in lean times.

beats.scene: A baby smiles while tasting something sweet from a spoon
beats.summary: People like sweet tastes from the very beginning of life, and sweetness once signalled ripe fruit and energy.

beats.scene: A child frowns and pushes away a spoonful of bitter green leaves
beats.summary: Bitter tastes often warn of harmful plants, which may be why many people find bitter greens harder to enjoy.

beats.scene: Fatty meat on a plate beside a pinch of salt
beats.summary: We are also drawn to fat and salt, which are useful to the body and were valuable and rare in the past.

beats.scene: A jar of honey beside a heap of sugar crystals
beats.summary: Honey was a rare treat, and sugar was an expensive luxury in much of the world until a few centuries ago.

beats.scene: A bright supermarket aisle full of packets, with a trolley in the middle
beats.summary: Today food is everywhere and cheap, so an old appetite meets a very modern food world.

beats.scene: Idris raises one hand while Noor tilts her head, thinking
beats.summary: Idris adds that scientists still debate the details; the story is a useful way to think, not proof of everything.

beats.scene: Noor turns the pages of her notebook, with evening times underlined in pencil
beats.summary: Noor sees that her cravings cluster in tired evenings, and Idris says the next step is to look inside the body.

beats.scene: Idris draws a stomach, a brain and an arrow on a paper napkin
beats.summary: Idris draws a simple picture: hunger is a message sent between the body and the brain.

beats.scene: A growling stomach drawn on a napkin with small wavy lines around it
beats.summary: Ghrelin, made mostly in the stomach, rises before meals and falls after eating.

beats.scene: A wall clock showing one o'clock above a lunch table with an empty plate
beats.summary: Ghrelin can follow routine, so a body used to meals at set times may start to expect them.

beats.scene: Noor at her desk glances at the clock while her stomach rumbles
beats.summary: Noor checks her notes and finds her hunger arrives at the same times each day, just as he described.

beats.scene: A cutaway drawing of a stomach stretching as food fills it
beats.summary: After eating, the stomach stretches and the gut sends signals to the brain that say enough.

beats.scene: A fast eater has an empty plate; a slow eater is halfway
beats.summary: Fullness signals need a little time to arrive, so someone who eats very fast can finish before the message does.

beats.scene: A body drawing labelled energy store
beats.summary: The body also keeps a long-term watch on its energy stores, using a hormone called leptin made by fat tissue.

beats.scene: Two hormone signs, ghrelin and leptin, pointing toward a drawing of a brain
beats.summary: Ghrelin and leptin are only two of many signals; the system is a conversation, not a pair of switches.

beats.scene: A glass of water beside a plate, with a hand pushing neither away
beats.summary: Appetite works like thirst: it is a need, and you cannot simply decide to switch it off.

beats.scene: Noor looks at an empty dinner plate beside an open biscuit tin
beats.summary: Idris separates real hunger from appetite for something particular, and Noor realises she often is not hungry at ten at night.

beats.scene: A drawing of a brain with a small star beside a plate of cake
beats.summary: The brain learns which foods feel rewarding and then wants them again.

beats.scene: Noor chews the fourth biscuit slowly while looking at the empty packet
beats.summary: Researchers separate wanting from liking: we can want a food a great deal without enjoying it much.

beats.scene: Warm bread and pastries in a bakery window with steam on the glass
beats.summary: Cues such as smells, sights and adverts can start the wanting before we have decided anything.

beats.scene: Noor walks past a bakery on Mill Street in the evening dusk
beats.summary: Noor notices her pastry habit follows a pattern: the bakery on her way home at the end of a tiring day.

beats.scene: Idris and Noor study a route map with the bakery circled
beats.summary: Idris explains that place, time and mood become cues, because the brain links them with the reward.

beats.scene: Noor walks a different street home, past a quiet park with trees
beats.summary: Noor tries an experiment: three days of walking home a different way, not as a punishment but to see what happens.

beats.scene: Noor sits on a park bench with her notebook open
beats.summary: On the first evening the wanting is strong, but by the third it is weaker, and she notes that it works for some cravings and not others.

beats.scene: Noor's phone on a table lights up with a food delivery message at night
beats.summary: Noor notices modern cues too: food adverts, videos and a delivery app that pings her in the evening.

beats.scene: Ocean waves rising and falling beneath a pale evening sky
beats.summary: Idris says cravings often rise and fade like a wave, so waiting a little can help.

beats.scene: A kitchen timer set to ten minutes beside a cup of tea
beats.summary: Noor tries waiting ten minutes with a cup of tea; sometimes the wanting fades and sometimes she eats, and both give information.

beats.scene: Idris puts a plain loaf and a brightly coloured snack packet on the table
beats.summary: Idris puts a plain loaf beside a snack packet and introduces the term ultra-processed.

beats.scene: Tins of tomatoes, frozen peas and a loaf of wholemeal bread on a shelf
beats.summary: Idris warns that not all processing is bad: tins, freezing and cooking help, and experts argue about where the lines fall.

beats.scene: People in white coats taste small samples at a table in a food laboratory
beats.summary: Many ultra-processed foods are carefully designed to be very appealing, with taste and texture tested again and again.

beats.scene: A hand takes a soft snack from a bag while scrolling a phone
beats.summary: Many such foods are soft and quick to swallow, so they can be eaten fast and in large amounts.

beats.scene: Volunteers eat meals at a long table in a quiet research centre
beats.summary: In one careful study, people ate more calories on a diet of mostly ultra-processed foods than on one of unprocessed food.

beats.scene: A question mark above a plate of snacks and a plate of whole food
beats.summary: Why this happened is not fully known; faster eating, soft texture and energy-dense food are possible reasons.

beats.scene: A table at a party covered with many different snacks and bowls
beats.summary: Variety makes us eat more: we tire of one taste but still have room for a new one.

beats.scene: A kitchen cupboard shelf crowded with half-open packets of biscuits and crisps
beats.summary: Noor sees that her cupboard is a small party table of half-open packets, while plain food gets boring and is easy to stop.

beats.scene: Noor reads the label on a packet in a bright supermarket aisle
beats.summary: Labels can mislead, and Idris says a short list of ordinary ingredients is a rough guide but no reason for panic.

beats.scene: Noor stands at a kitchen counter with a bowl of nuts and an apple
beats.summary: Noor learns this is not about weakness but about clever design; the answer is more whole foods most days, without panic.

beats.scene: Idris stirs a pot of red lentil soup on Noor's small stove
beats.summary: Idris cooks lentil soup in Noor's kitchen and says some foods fill us up more than others for the same energy.

beats.scene: Oats, beans and vegetables arranged on a wooden board
beats.summary: Fibre is the part of plants we cannot fully digest; it adds bulk and slows digestion, and it is found in oats, beans and vegetables.

beats.scene: A plate with an egg, a piece of fish and a bowl of beans
beats.summary: Protein tends to fill us more than the same amount of energy from other nutrients, and it is found in eggs, fish, beans and dairy.

beats.scene: A steaming bowl of vegetable soup beside a plate of pastry
beats.summary: Foods with a lot of water, like soup, fruit and vegetables, add volume for little energy and help us feel full.

beats.scene: A whole orange beside a glass of orange juice on a table
beats.summary: Whole fruit fills us more than juice, because it has fibre and takes longer to eat.

beats.scene: A tall sweet coffee beside a half-eaten sandwich on a desk
beats.summary: Sugary drinks tend to fill us less than solid food, so their energy is easy to miss.

beats.scene: Two breakfast bowls: oat porridge and sugary cereal
beats.summary: Noor tries porridge one day and sugary cereal the next, and notes how hungry she is by eleven.

beats.scene: A notebook page with two columns of notes
beats.summary: The porridge morning leaves her steadier; Idris says one test is not proof, but it is her own evidence.

beats.scene: A small pile of nuts beside a large pile of vegetables
beats.summary: Idris explains energy density: vegetables hold little energy per bite and oils or pastry hold a lot, yet rich foods like nuts can be healthy too.

beats.scene: Noor eats a dinner of lentil soup, bread and salad at a small table
beats.summary: Idris offers a simple picture, not a rule: vegetables, some protein and a fibre-rich starch; Noor feels quieter that evening.

beats.scene: Noor holds an enormous family-size packet of crisps in a supermarket aisle
beats.summary: Noor sees a giant packet on offer, and Idris explains that people tend to eat more from bigger portions.

beats.scene: A large and a small bucket of popcorn at a cinema counter
beats.summary: The effect appears with many foods and packet sizes, and the larger share is not always more enjoyed.

beats.scene: The same pasta on a small plate and a large plate
beats.summary: Plate size may change how much looks like enough, though studies are mixed, so a smaller plate is a cheap thing to try.

beats.scene: Noor pours crisps from a packet into a small bowl at a desk
beats.summary: Eating from a packet has no visible end, so Noor pours a portion into a bowl and notices when she is finished.

beats.scene: A diner faces a very large plate of food
beats.summary: Portions in restaurants and takeaways are often large, and people tend to feel they should finish what they are given.

beats.scene: A child at a table with a half-eaten plate while a parent watches
beats.summary: Many people learned as children to finish their plate, which teaches us to ignore fullness; it is fine to leave food or save it.

beats.scene: Noor eats at her desk with her eyes on a laptop
beats.summary: Eating while distracted by a screen can lead to eating more and noticing less.

beats.scene: An empty crisp bowl beside a laptop with a puzzled Noor looking at it
beats.summary: Noor finds that on screen evenings she cannot recall eating the crisps at all, and the bowl is empty.

beats.scene: Friends laugh around a shared table with plates of food in the middle
beats.summary: People often eat more in company, and match each other's pace, so who we eat with also shapes how much we eat.

beats.scene: Noor eats vegetables and rice at a table, her phone face down
beats.summary: For a week Noor eats dinner at a table without a screen; it takes longer, tastes better, and she forgets on some nights.

beats.scene: Noor yawns at her kitchen table with a mug of coffee at breakfast
beats.summary: Noor yawns through a breakfast chat, and Idris asks how she has been sleeping.

beats.scene: A clock showing three beside a bed and a glass of water
beats.summary: In experiments, people who sleep too little tend to feel hungrier and to want richer food.

beats.scene: A notebook page with moons drawn beside the days of her worst cravings
beats.summary: Noor checks her notebook and finds her strongest cravings follow her shortest nights.

beats.scene: A tired Noor stares at a plate of cake with half-closed eyes
beats.summary: A tired brain responds more strongly to tempting food and has less energy for restraint.

beats.scene: A coffee cup and a chocolate bar on an office desk
beats.summary: Tiredness leads to a cycle: sugar and caffeine for quick energy, which can make sleep worse again.

beats.scene: Noor lies in bed in the dark with her face lit by a phone
beats.summary: Bright screens late at night can delay sleep, and Noor sees that she scrolls in bed far later than she means to.

beats.scene: A kitchen at night with a single light on and a half-eaten sandwich
beats.summary: Eating a big meal very late may disturb sleep for some people, and late-night eating is often snacking.

beats.scene: A dark quiet bedroom with a closed curtain and an alarm clock
beats.summary: Idris shares sleep basics: regular times, a dark and cool room, and caffeine earlier in the day; a doctor can help with long-term sleep trouble.

beats.scene: A night nurse in uniform eats a sandwich in a quiet hospital corridor
beats.summary: Idris remembers night-shift patients, whose body clocks make eating well harder, and who need kindness and a plan.

beats.scene: Noor switches off her lamp; her phone charges across the room
beats.summary: Noor tries an earlier bedtime for a week; the evening cravings grow quieter, though not gone.

beats.scene: Noor and Hana at office desks with papers and a sweet jar
beats.summary: A deadline week at the office makes Noor eat more sweets, from the jar on her colleague Hana's desk.

beats.scene: Idris reads Noor's anxious notebook entries through his glasses
beats.summary: Stress changes appetite: for many people it increases the wish for comfort food, though some lose their appetite instead.

beats.scene: A bowl of warm macaroni and cheese steaming on a table
beats.summary: Rich, sweet or fatty food can feel soothing in the moment, which is why comfort foods are so named.

beats.scene: A mother hugs a child and gives her a biscuit
beats.summary: Many of us learned as children to link food with feeling better: a sweet after a fall, a treat for being brave.

beats.scene: A slow rising wave and a sudden lightning bolt drawn on paper
beats.summary: Hunger from the body usually builds gradually and accepts many foods; emotional hunger often arrives suddenly and wants one thing.

beats.scene: Noor writes one word, tired, in her notebook beside a time and a place
beats.summary: Noor tries pausing to name the feeling before eating, and finds that naming it often makes it feel smaller.

beats.scene: A list headed Comforts: tea, a walk, music, a phone call
beats.summary: Idris suggests a menu of comforts alongside food: a walk, music, a warm shower, a call to a friend.

beats.scene: Noor and Hana walk side by side along a street at lunchtime
beats.summary: Hana admits she hides chocolate in a drawer too; they laugh and agree to take a walk each afternoon.

beats.scene: Idris pours tea for Noor while she nibbles a single biscuit on a saucer
beats.summary: Idris says a biscuit with tea in a hard moment is normal and human; it is a problem only if it is the only tool or causes distress.

beats.scene: Noor in an armchair with tea and one biscuit
beats.summary: On her next bad day Noor eats a biscuit slowly with tea, then goes for a walk, and writes that she was kind to herself.

beats.scene: Idris draws a circle with three arrows labelled trigger, action and payoff
beats.summary: Habits form a loop: a trigger, an action and a payoff, and repeating it makes it automatic.

beats.scene: Noor draws her loop: tired walk, pastry, relief
beats.summary: Noor draws her own loop: a tired walk home, a pastry from the bakery, and a few minutes of relief.

beats.scene: A driver on a familiar road at dusk, hands relaxed on the steering wheel
beats.summary: The brain makes repeated actions automatic to save effort, like driving a road you know without thinking.

beats.scene: A footpath worn into a green lawn beside a new, faint path
beats.summary: Old habits do not vanish; it is usually easier to build a new loop than to erase the old one.

beats.scene: Noor sits on a park bench with a flask of tea
beats.summary: Idris suggests keeping the trigger and the payoff and changing only the action: a flask of tea on a park bench.

beats.scene: A handwritten if-then plan card in Noor's hand
beats.summary: Noor writes an if-then plan: if she feels the pull at the bakery door, then she walks on to the park bench.

beats.scene: A single apple placed next to a toaster on the kitchen counter
beats.summary: Idris says the biggest mistake is to aim too big; a new habit should be so small that it is almost easy.

beats.scene: A calendar with a long row of days and small ticks
beats.summary: In one study, habits took about two months to feel automatic on average, but with a huge spread from weeks to many months.

beats.scene: Noor sticks a gold star on a wall calendar in a bright kitchen
beats.summary: Noor sticks a star on her calendar for each park-bench day, because feeling good about a habit helps it stick.

beats.scene: Noor stands at the bakery window, hungry and thoughtful
beats.summary: On day nine Noor buys a pastry anyway; she writes what triggered it, without blame, and carries on.

beats.scene: Noor sighs at the kitchen table over a cold cup of tea
beats.summary: Noor says she just needs more willpower, and Idris asks her what willpower actually is.

beats.scene: A battery symbol drawn on the napkin, nearly empty, beside the word evening
beats.summary: Willpower is weaker when we are tired, hungry or stressed, and in many people it is thinnest in the evening.

beats.scene: A scientist with a clipboard looks puzzled at a chart with a question mark
beats.summary: Scientists still debate how willpower works, and a famous idea that it is a limited fuel has been questioned, but tired, hungry people do struggle.

beats.scene: A long to-do list on a phone beside a weary commuter on a train
beats.summary: Every day is full of small choices, and a long day of decisions can leave little patience for the last one.

beats.scene: Noor writes a dinner plan in a notebook at a bright breakfast table
beats.summary: Since willpower is weak at night, it is wiser to plan in the morning, when we are calm and rested.

beats.scene: A person walks past a shop window full of cakes without looking in
beats.summary: Studies of people with good self-control suggest they often avoid temptation rather than resist it again and again.

beats.scene: A biscuit tin on a high shelf and a fruit bowl on the counter
beats.summary: Make the healthy choice the easy choice: add a few steps to the one you want less, and remove steps from the one you want more.

beats.scene: A hungry shopper stares at a long supermarket shelf of packaged sweets
beats.summary: Hungry people make different choices, so big decisions about food are best made when we are not hungry.

beats.scene: A card on the fridge door headed Tired Evening Plan, with four short lines
beats.summary: Noor writes a tired-evening plan: dinner ready by seven, a cup of tea, a short shower, and no cupboard until the morning.

beats.scene: Noor crosses the word weak out of her notebook with a firm line
beats.summary: Idris says guilt is not fuel; harsh self-criticism drains us, and Noor decides to stop calling herself weak.

beats.scene: Idris stands in the doorway of Noor's kitchen and looks around slowly
beats.summary: Idris asks Noor what she sees first when she enters her kitchen, and explains that we eat what we see and reach easily.

beats.scene: A dish of sweets on one desk, a closed drawer on another
beats.summary: In experiments in offices and canteens, people tended to take and eat more food when it was visible and close, and less when it was hidden or far away.

beats.scene: Noor puts apples on the counter and a tin in a high cupboard
beats.summary: Noor rearranges her kitchen: fruit in view, biscuits in a high cupboard.

beats.scene: Noor stands on a small stool reaching into a high cupboard
beats.summary: The tin is not banned: she can still reach it, but it now takes a stool and a decision, and the pause is the point.

beats.scene: Clear boxes of chopped carrots, hummus and beans at the front of a fridge
beats.summary: In the fridge, ready-to-eat foods go at the front at eye level: cut vegetables, hummus, cooked beans and leftovers in clear boxes.

beats.scene: A supermarket checkout lane lined with chocolate bars and magazines
beats.summary: Supermarkets are arranged to sell, with special displays and sweets near the tills, so shopping needs a little plan.

beats.scene: Noor walks down a supermarket aisle with a short list in her hand
beats.summary: Shopping after a meal and with a list helps us buy what we planned, so Noor goes after dinner with a short list.

beats.scene: Noor sits at a laptop adding vegetables to an online shopping basket
beats.summary: Online shopping can have fewer displays, but saved favourites can be easy to reorder, so a list still helps.

beats.scene: A small chocolate bar beside an apple on a kitchen windowsill
beats.summary: Idris suggests keeping big treats outside the home and buying small treats on purpose, so having a treat takes a decision.

beats.scene: Hana looks around Noor's bright kitchen with a bowl of fruit and a calendar
beats.summary: Hana visits and says the kitchen looks like a different flat; the notebook shows fewer late entries, though not none.

beats.scene: Noor holds up an old magazine diet plan with a coloured chart
beats.summary: Noor shows Idris the magazine diet she once followed, and describes how it began well and ended with a rebound.

beats.scene: A drawing of a body with a large arrow showing hunger rising
beats.summary: Very strict diets can backfire: when someone loses weight quickly, the body raises hunger and lowers fullness signals.

beats.scene: A candle burning low with a small flame beside a thermometer drawing
beats.summary: The body may also adapt by using a little less energy, which makes steady loss harder.

beats.scene: A small boy stares at a cookie jar on a high shelf with longing
beats.summary: Strict rules can make a forbidden food seem bigger in the mind, so people think about it more and want it more.

beats.scene: A long road with a signpost for a diet and a tired traveller
beats.summary: Many people who lose weight on strict plans regain it over the years, which is a sign of how hard the body pushes back, not of a weak mind.

beats.scene: A person looks at a ruined cake on a table with a tired shrug
beats.summary: All-or-nothing thinking turns a small slip into a collapse: scientists call it the what-the-hell effect.

beats.scene: A week drawn as a grid of twenty-one meals with one square coloured differently
beats.summary: One biscuit does not ruin a week: a week has about twenty-one meals, and one treat is a small part.

beats.scene: Noor eats a slice of cake with a friend, smiling
beats.summary: Flexible approaches that allow some treats seem to go with better long-term habits than very rigid rules.

beats.scene: A plate of toast and eggs at a breakfast table on a sunny morning
beats.summary: After a slip, restart at the next meal, not on Monday; Noor learns the next-meal rule.

beats.scene: A bottle labelled detox beside a clock and a wary cartoon face
beats.summary: Idris warns against extreme fasts and detoxes: any plan that promises a new life in a week is worth doubting, and a doctor should advise anyone with a medical condition.

beats.scene: Noor counts coins on a kitchen table beside a grocery receipt
beats.summary: Noor says healthy food seems expensive and time-consuming, and Idris agrees that eating well depends on money, time and what is sold nearby.

beats.scene: A street with many fast-food signs and only one small greengrocer
beats.summary: Neighbourhoods differ: some have many fast-food outlets and few fresh food shops, and people tend to eat what is near.

beats.scene: Noor leaves her flat past a fried chicken shop and a corner store
beats.summary: Noor looks at her own street: a fast-food shop, a corner store and a supermarket fifteen minutes away by bus.

beats.scene: Mrs Farah stands behind a busy market stall piled with lentils and onions
beats.summary: At the Saturday market Mrs Farah, a stallholder, sells lentils, onions and greens, and teaches Noor to buy what is in season.

beats.scene: A table showing beans, lentils, oats, eggs, frozen vegetables and tinned fish
beats.summary: Many healthy foods are cheap: beans, lentils, oats, eggs, frozen vegetables and tinned fish.

beats.scene: Frozen peas, a tin of tomatoes and a tin of sardines
beats.summary: Frozen and tinned foods are often as nutritious as fresh ones, and they waste less; rinsing tinned beans lowers the salt.

beats.scene: Noor compares two jars of lentils on a shelf, reading the price per kilo
beats.summary: Budget tips: compare the price per kilo, try cheaper own-brand versions, cook from scratch, and plan meals to avoid waste.

beats.scene: Noor cooks eggs, spinach and tomatoes in a single frying pan
beats.summary: Simple cooking in one pan makes a healthy meal quick enough for a busy evening.

beats.scene: Containers of lentil stew cool on a counter beside a freezer drawer
beats.summary: Noor cooks a big pot of lentil stew on Sunday and freezes portions, so a good dinner is always waiting.

beats.scene: Idris and Noor sit at the market café while shoppers pass with heavy bags
beats.summary: Idris admits that some people cannot afford enough good food, and says this is a matter of shops, wages and time, and help exists for those in need.

beats.scene: Noor reads an invitation message on her phone with a worried face
beats.summary: Noor is invited to her Auntie Leila's big Sunday lunch and worries about how she will manage there.

beats.scene: Idris and Noor on a park bench, with a picnic basket between them
beats.summary: Idris explains that food is also love and belonging: in many families, feeding people is how care is shown.

beats.scene: A long family table crowded with dishes, with Auntie Leila holding a serving spoon
beats.summary: At Auntie Leila's table there is far too much food, and Noor hears Eat, eat, and feels torn between her plan and her aunt.

beats.scene: Noor takes a small first helping while her aunt looks on with a smile
beats.summary: Idris's tips: take a smaller first plate, praise the cook warmly, and ask to take leftovers home.

beats.scene: A pot of rice with beans and vegetables steams on a family stove
beats.summary: Traditions matter and need not be changed; small tweaks like more beans and vegetables keep the flavours.

beats.scene: Colleagues round an office birthday cake; one hand waves it away
beats.summary: Social pressure at birthdays and at work, with cries of go on, just one, can be met with a warm yes or a friendly no, without explanation.

beats.scene: A billboard showing a giant burger beside a smiling child
beats.summary: Food companies spend large sums on advertising, especially to children, and it works.

beats.scene: Noor counts food adverts on a bus shelter, a screen and a magazine

beats.scene: Sami's small daughter Yara points at a cereal box with a cartoon tiger
beats.summary: Noor's brother Sami says his daughter Yara begs for the cereal with a cartoon on the box, and Idris says children are especially open to persuasion.

beats.scene: Noor leaves Leila's house carrying a box of leftovers while Leila waves
beats.summary: At the lunch Noor takes a small first plate, praises the stew, and takes leftovers home; Leila beams, and it is the best meal in weeks.

beats.summary: Yara refuses broccoli again, and Idris explains that children often need to try a new food many times before they like it.

beats.summary: Noor admits that she hated cabbage as a child, and Idris says adults' tastes can change too.

beats.summary: Many people find that after cutting down on sugar for a few weeks, sweet things taste sweeter; Noor halves the sugar in her tea.

beats.scene: A salt shaker beside fresh herbs and ground spices

beats.scene: A tray of roasted carrots and cauliflower with brown edges, fresh from an oven
beats.summary: Healthy food needs to taste good: roasting, herbs and spices make vegetables delicious; Idris roasts carrots and cauliflower with cumin.

beats.scene: A lemon half, salt and olive oil beside raw greens
beats.summary: Idris shares tricks for bitter greens: a little salt, olive oil, lemon, or roasting, which softens bitterness.

beats.scene: Noor stirs chopped spinach into a pan of scrambled eggs
beats.summary: Adding a healthy food is easier than banning a favourite one, so Noor stirs spinach into her morning eggs.

beats.scene: Yara holds a small piece of broccoli on a fork while her father watches

beats.scene: A drawn timeline of Noor's day with a tiny lunch and a huge evening
beats.summary: Noor maps her day: no breakfast, a small lunch, and a huge hunger by evening.

beats.scene: A breakfast table with porridge, boiled eggs and yoghurt with fruit
beats.summary: Noor lines up easy breakfasts: porridge, eggs, yoghurt with fruit, or wholemeal toast with beans.

beats.scene: Noor eats leftover lentil stew from a box at her office desk

beats.scene: A small bag of nuts and an apple on Noor's desk at four o'clock

beats.summary: Idris gives Noor a raisin to eat very slowly, so she can notice what attention does to taste.

beats.scene: A glass of water on a kitchen table next to a clock showing four
beats.summary: A glass of water is a cheap check: thirst and hunger can feel similar for some people, so drink and wait a few minutes.

beats.scene: A glass of wine beside a bowl of salty snacks
beats.summary: Alcohol can lower our caution and tends to go with snacking, so evening drinks are another thing to notice.

beats.scene: Noor's day drawn as a calm timeline with four meals and a small snack
beats.summary: Noor's new rhythm is breakfast, lunch, a snack and dinner, and her late hunger arrives less often; rhythms differ, and the plan can bend.

beats.scene: A small plate with one square of chocolate beside a lit candle
beats.summary: Treats are not forbidden, but they are better enjoyed slowly and on purpose.

beats.scene: Noor at a table with a slice of cake and a fork

beats.scene: Noor and Hana look at a menu in a small restaurant, pointing at dishes

beats.summary: Holidays, weddings and busy weeks will interrupt any plan, so Noor goes to Hana's wedding week and eats freely without guilt.

beats.scene: Noor stands before a nearly empty fridge on a Sunday morning, writing a list
beats.summary: After the trip and the cold, Noor restarts with one small step: she shops and plans one good meal, not the whole week.

beats.scene: Idris and Noor review the green notebook together at the kitchen table
beats.summary: Idris and Noor review the notebook: keep what works, drop what does not, because the plan should fit her life and bend, not break.

beats.scene: Hana shows Noor a phone screen with a fashionable diet plan at lunchtime
beats.summary: Hana starts a fashionable diet and loves it, and Noor wonders whether she should copy her friend.

beats.scene: Four different people eat the same bowl of porridge with different expressions
beats.summary: Bodies differ because of genes, gut microbes, age, sleep, medicines and history; people can respond differently even to the same meal.

beats.scene: Noor opens her notebook beside two plates of food that look the same
beats.summary: So what works for a friend may not work for you, and Noor's notebook is the right tool to find out what works for her.

beats.scene: Idris holds up four fingers beside a phone showing a smiling influencer
beats.summary: Idris offers four questions for any new food claim: who benefits, what is the evidence, is it extreme, and can you keep it up for years.

beats.scene: A long winding path with a small figure walking steadily toward green hills
beats.summary: The best plan is the one you can keep; many different eating patterns can work if they suit you and are sustained.

beats.scene: A bathroom scale pushed into a cupboard beside a pair of walking shoes
beats.summary: Eating good food matters for health in itself, so Noor focuses on habits, energy and mood, not only on the number on the scale.

beats.scene: Noor and Hana walk quickly along a river path in the morning light
beats.summary: Movement you enjoy helps health and mood, but it is not a punishment for eating; Noor and Hana keep walking.

beats.scene: Noor looks into a mirror with a soft, steady expression
beats.summary: Shame tends to backfire, while self-kindness supports lasting change, and people who are kind to themselves after a slip tend to recover faster.

beats.scene: Noor deletes a social media app from her phone as a sunrise glows outside

beats.scene: Noor writes a note at the kitchen table with a mug of tea
beats.summary: Noor writes a short note to the woman she was at the fridge on that first night: you were not weak, you did not know yet.

beats.scene: Idris sits beside Noor on a sofa, speaking gently with his hands open
beats.summary: Idris explains that if eating feels out of control, very restricted, or brings constant worry, a doctor can help.

beats.scene: A doctor and a dietitian talk with a patient in a bright clinic room
beats.summary: People with medical conditions, allergies, pregnancy or special needs, and parents with worries about a child, need advice made for them.

beats.scene: Idris at a table at midnight with a piece of chocolate
beats.summary: Idris confesses that he too once ate chocolate at midnight in his first year of retirement, and Noor laughs with relief.

beats.scene: Noor's notebook pages from the first week and the latest week side by side

beats.scene: A card pinned beside the fridge listing five small changes in Noor's handwriting
beats.summary: Noor sums up the small changes that fit her life: a plan, a helpful kitchen, satisfying food, enough sleep and a kind voice.

beats.scene: Yara and Noor roast carrots together in a bright kitchen
beats.summary: Sami and Yara visit, and Noor shows Yara how to roast carrots, passing on the lesson with no lecture.

beats.scene: Noor hands Hana a small new notebook with a bow of ribbon on it
beats.summary: Hana grows tired of her strict diet and asks Noor for advice, and Noor gives her a small notebook, just as Idris once did.

beats.scene: Noor stands calmly at the open fridge late at night

beats.scene: Idris stands by a window watching Noor cook
beats.summary: Idris says that healthy eating is hard because of an old appetite in a modern world, and that small steps work better than heroic ones.

beats.scene: Noor and Idris sit at the kitchen table as the light fades

B1B2: Noor planned a healthy dinner, but at ten o'clock she is standing at the open fridge. She wants a biscuit, and she cannot understand why eating well feels so hard.
At work the next morning, Noor opens a note on her phone called Plans. It lists a salad week, a month without sugar and a diet from a magazine, and every one of them ended in failure.
Noor remembers that her uncle Idris spent forty years working as a dietitian. At lunchtime she phones him and admits, a little shyly, that she needs some help with food.
On Saturday Idris arrives at her small flat with a bag of oranges and a tin of tea. He sits at her kitchen table and lets her tell the whole story without interrupting once.
When she has finished, Idris smiles and says that wanting biscuits is not a weakness. Appetite is a very old piece of machinery, he explains, and it is simply doing the job it was built to do.

Idris tells her about his forty years in hospitals and clinics, where he met thousands of people. Almost all of them already knew which foods were healthy, he says, and still found it hard to eat them.
Noor protests that she knows exactly what a healthy dinner looks like, and she even enjoys cooking one. Idris nods and says that this is the very point: knowing and doing are two different skills.
Idris promises that he will not scold her or hand her a diet sheet. Instead they will be curious, like two detectives, and ask when the wanting comes, why it comes and how she feels.
Before he leaves, Idris gives her a small green notebook and a pencil. She is not to count calories or to judge herself, he says, only to write down when the wanting arrives.
That evening Noor eats a biscuit, as she usually does, but this time she writes down the time and how she feels. To her surprise she feels curious instead of ashamed.
A week later Idris comes back, and Noor shows him the notebook. He begins his story far back in time, in a world where nobody knew when the next meal would come.
For most of human history, people spent long days looking for berries, roots, nuts and meat. Some days they found plenty, and on other days they found almost nothing at all.
Many scientists think that people who enjoyed rich, filling food had an advantage in hard times. Their bodies stored some energy as fat, and that stored energy helped them through the lean days.
Studies show that newborn babies seem to like sweet tastes, even before they have tried much food. In nature, sweetness usually means ripe fruit, and ripe fruit means energy.
Bitter tastes are different, because in nature they can be a warning that a plant is harmful. This may be one reason why many children, and some adults, find leafy greens hard to enjoy.
We are drawn to fat and salt as well. Fat holds a lot of energy, and the body needs some salt, but both were hard to find for many of our ancestors.
Honey was a rare and sometimes dangerous prize, because bees do not give it up easily. Sugar was an expensive luxury in much of Europe for centuries, and only became cheap quite recently.
Today Noor can find sweet, fatty and salty food on every street corner, and it costs very little effort. An appetite built for scarcity now lives in a world of plenty.
Idris is careful to say that scientists still debate many details of this story. It is a useful way of thinking about appetite, he says, but it is not proof of everything.
Looking at her notebook, Noor sees that her cravings come mostly on tired evenings and rarely at lunchtime. Idris says this is useful, and that next they should look at what happens inside the body.
Idris takes a paper napkin and draws a stomach, a brain and a line between them. Hunger is not a feeling that appears from nowhere, he says, but a message that travels between the body and the brain.
One of the messengers is a hormone called ghrelin, which is made mostly in the stomach. Its level rises before a meal, and it falls again after we have eaten.
Ghrelin also follows our daily routines and our habits of eating. If we usually eat lunch at one o'clock, many people find that their hunger arrives at about that time.
Noor looks at her notebook and finds that she is hungry at much the same times every day. Her stomach starts to rumble at about one o'clock, and again at four.
After a meal, the stomach stretches, and the gut sends signals to the brain that say, enough for now. These signals are made of both nerves and hormones, and they work together.
The fullness signals do not arrive at once, because they need a little time to build. A very fast eater can finish a large meal before the message reaches the brain.
The body also keeps a long-term watch on its energy stores, using a hormone called leptin. Leptin is made by fat tissue, and it tells the brain how much energy the body is carrying.
Ghrelin and leptin are only two voices among many in this conversation. Scientists have found many other signals, and they are still learning how all of them fit together.
Idris says that appetite is very much like thirst. You can ignore it for a while, but it is a real need, and nobody can simply decide to switch it off.
Idris explains that hunger and appetite are not quite the same thing. Hunger is the body asking for fuel, but appetite is a wish for one food, and Noor has often just eaten dinner.
When we eat something tasty, the brain's reward system takes note. The next time we meet that food, it pushes us gently to have it again.
Researchers have found that wanting and liking are not the same thing. Noor realises that by the fourth biscuit she wants it badly, yet she hardly tastes it.
Smells, sights and sounds can start the wanting before we have decided anything at all. The smell of baking bread is a famous example, but a food advert can do the same.
Noor reads her notebook again and spots a pattern. On the tiring days she often buys a pastry at the bakery on Mill Street, which she passes on her way home.
Idris explains that the place, the time of day and our mood can all become cues. The brain links them with the reward, so the bakery doorway starts the wanting all by itself.
Idris suggests an experiment and not a punishment for her at all. For three days Noor walks home by a different street, past a park, and writes down what happens.
On the first evening the wanting is strong, and she nearly turns back. By the third day it is much weaker, although she notes that the biscuits at home still call her.
Noor notices that her phone is full of cues, too. A food video appears in the evening, and a delivery app sends her a message just when she is tired.
Idris tells her that a craving often behaves like a wave. It rises, reaches a peak and then fades, and many people find that it passes within a short time if they let it.
The next evening Noor sets a timer for ten minutes and makes a cup of tea. Sometimes the craving fades, and sometimes she eats the biscuit anyway, and Idris says both results teach her something.

Idris places a plain loaf of bread next to a bright snack packet. Some researchers use the word ultra-processed for foods that are made in factories from many ingredients, and the packet is one of them.
Idris is careful to add that processing is not always bad. Freezing peas, tinning tomatoes and baking bread are all forms of processing, and experts still argue about where the lines should be drawn.
Many of these foods are designed to be very appealing. Companies test the sweetness, the saltiness and the crunch again and again, until the product is hard to resist.
Many of these foods are soft, crisp or crumbly, and they melt in the mouth with very little chewing. We can eat a lot of them very quickly before the fullness signals have time to arrive.
In one careful study, adults lived at a research centre and ate two different diets, each for two weeks. On the diet of mostly ultra-processed foods they ate about five hundred more calories a day.
Scientists are still not certain why people ate more on that diet. Faster eating, soft textures and food that packs a lot of energy into a small bite may all play a part.
Variety makes us eat more, because we tire of one taste but still have room for a new one. That is why a party table full of different snacks is so easy to keep eating from.

Back home, Noor opens her cupboard and sees six half-open packets, each with a different taste. Her cupboard is a small party table, while plain foods like boiled rice soon feel boring and are easy to stop eating.

Idris tells her that labels such as natural, light or high in protein do not always mean healthy. A short list of ordinary ingredients is a rough guide, but it is no reason to panic about every packet.
Noor sees that she was not weak, because clever people designed these foods to be easy to eat. The calm answer, Idris says, is to eat more whole foods on most days, without any panic.
Idris arrives with a bag of red lentils and cooks soup in Noor's small kitchen. Some foods fill us up much more than others, he says, even when they hold the same amount of energy.
Fibre is the part of plants that our bodies cannot fully digest. It adds bulk and slows down digestion, and it is found in beans, oats, vegetables and fruit.
The second reason is protein, which Idris explains next with an egg in his hand. In many studies it seems to fill people up more than other nutrients, and it is found in eggs, fish, beans and meat.
The third reason is simply the water in food. Soups, fruit and vegetables hold a lot of water, so they fill the stomach and feel like a big meal, with fairly little energy.
Idris peels an orange and puts it next to a glass of orange juice. The whole fruit has fibre and takes time to chew, so it usually fills you up much more than the juice.
Drinks with sugar tend to fill us up less than solid food does. Their energy is easy to miss, and Noor realises that her afternoon sweet coffee holds more than she thought.
Idris asks Noor to run a small test of her own. She eats porridge one morning and sugary cereal the next, and she writes down how hungry she feels at eleven o'clock.
The porridge morning goes better, and she stays satisfied until lunch. Idris says that one test is not proof, but it is her own evidence, and that is worth a great deal.
Idris explains energy density, which means how much energy is in each bite. Vegetables have little and pastry or oil have a lot, but rich foods such as nuts can still be very healthy.
Idris offers a simple picture for dinner: some vegetables, some protein and a starchy food with plenty of fibre. It is a picture and not a rule, and that evening Noor feels full and much quieter.
In the supermarket Noor picks up a giant packet that is on special offer. Idris tells her that people tend to eat more when the portion in front of them is bigger.
The effect appears with many kinds of food, from snacks to main meals. People who are given more often finish more, even if they do not enjoy the extra food any better.
Some studies suggest that a big plate makes a portion look smaller, so we serve ourselves more. The results are mixed, though, and Idris says a smaller plate is simply a cheap thing to try.
When we eat straight from a packet, there is no clear end to it, and the bottom arrives as a surprise. Noor tries pouring a portion into a bowl, and she notices when she has finished.
Portions in restaurants and takeaways are often large, and many people have noticed that sizes have grown over the years. We tend to feel that we should finish whatever is put in front of us.
Many of us were taught as children to finish everything on our plates. That habit can teach us to ignore our fullness, and Idris says it is fine to leave food or save it for later.
Noor often eats her dinner in front of a screen. Idris explains that eating while distracted can lead us to eat more and notice less.
Noor reads her notebook and finds that on her evenings with a screen she often cannot remember eating the crisps. She just looks down, surprised, and the bowl is empty.
People often eat more when they eat with friends or family, and they tend to match each other's pace. Who we eat with, and how long the meal lasts, can change how much we eat.
For one week Noor eats her dinner at the table with her phone turned face down. It takes her longer and the food tastes better, although on two nights she forgets and ends up back at the desk.

Idris says that when people in experiments sleep too little, they often feel hungrier the next day. They also tend to want richer food, and some studies find changes in hunger hormones too.
Noor looks through her notebook for the last month. On the days that follow her shortest nights, her cravings are the strongest, and the biscuit tin seems to call much louder.
Some brain studies suggest that tired people respond more strongly to pictures of tempting food. A tired brain also has less energy for saying no, so the cake feels harder to refuse.
When we are tired, we often look for quick energy in sugar and caffeine. If the coffee comes late in the day, it can make the next night's sleep worse, and the cycle begins again.
Bright screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep, and the endless scrolling keeps the mind busy. Noor sees that she often looks at her phone in bed for an hour after she meant to sleep.

For some people a large meal very late at night makes it harder to sleep well. Late-night eating is also often snacking in front of a screen, which brings back everything they learned about distraction.
Idris shares a few sleep basics: similar bedtimes, a dark and cool room and caffeine earlier in the day. If sleep trouble goes on for a long time, he adds, a doctor can help.

Idris remembers the night-shift workers he used to help, such as nurses and bus drivers. Their body clocks are out of step with the world, so eating well is harder for them, and they need kindness and a plan.
For one week Noor goes to bed by eleven, with her phone charging across the room. Her evening cravings are quieter, though they have not gone away, and she feels better in the morning.
It is deadline week at the office, and Noor is staying late every evening. Her colleague Hana keeps a jar of sweets on her desk, and Noor takes one every hour without noticing.

Rich, sweet or fatty food can feel soothing in the moment, which is exactly why we call it comfort food. The relief is real, but it often fades faster than the worry does.

Idris says that hunger from the body usually builds gradually and would accept many different foods. Hunger from emotions often arrives suddenly, wants one particular thing and does not feel finished when the plate is empty.
Before she eats, Noor tries to stop and name the feeling, such as tired, lonely or worried. Many people find that putting a name on a feeling makes it a little smaller and easier to handle.
Idris suggests that Noor writes a list of other comforts that she can use alongside food. A walk, some music, a warm shower or a phone call to a friend are all good choices.
When Noor tells Hana about her notebook, Hana laughs and admits that she hides chocolate in her drawer. They agree to take a short walk together every afternoon instead of reaching for the jar.
Idris says that a biscuit with a cup of tea in a hard moment is a very human thing to do. It is only a problem if food is the one and only tool, or if it leaves us feeling distressed.

On her next bad day, Noor sits down with a cup of tea and one biscuit, and she eats it slowly. Then she puts on her shoes and goes for a walk, and she writes in the notebook that she was kind to herself.
Idris draws a circle with three arrows and names each one: trigger, action and payoff. A habit, he says, is a loop that we repeat until it becomes automatic.

Old habits rarely disappear completely, and Idris says that the old loop is still there in the brain. It is usually easier to build a new path next to it than to try to erase it.

Noor writes an if-then plan on a card: if I feel the pull at the bakery door, then I walk on to the bench. Research suggests that such specific plans help people to follow through.
Idris says that the biggest mistake is to aim too big at the start. A new habit should be so small that it feels almost too easy, such as adding one piece of fruit to breakfast.

On the ninth day Noor buys a pastry anyway, because it has been a terrible day. She does not blame herself; she writes down what set it off and carries on the next evening.

A normal day is full of small choices, from what to wear to what to answer in an email. After a long day of decisions, there may be little patience left for the last one at night.
Idris says that the wise answer is to plan, not to rely on willpower. A plan made in the morning, when we are calm and rested, is worth more than a heroic effort at ten o'clock at night.
Some studies of people with good self-control give a surprising result. They often are not heroes of resistance, but people who arrange their lives so that they meet fewer temptations.
Idris says to make the healthy choice the easy one. If a food takes five more steps to reach, we eat it less, but a food right in front of us gets eaten more.

Noor writes a plan for her tired evenings and sticks it to the fridge. It says that dinner is ready by seven, then a cup of tea and a short shower, and no opening the cupboard.

Idris stands in the doorway of her kitchen and asks what she sees first. What we can see and reach easily is what we tend to eat, he explains, so the setting of a kitchen matters.
In experiments in offices and canteens, people tended to eat more when food was in plain view and close at hand. They ate less when it was hidden in a drawer or placed across the room.

Noor arranges the fridge in the same way, too, as Idris suggests. She puts cut vegetables, hummus and cooked beans at the front, and she keeps leftovers in clear boxes where she can see them.
Idris reminds Noor that a supermarket is arranged to sell things, not to help her plan her week. Special displays, sweets near the tills and bright offers all catch the eye.
Shopping after a meal and with a list helps us buy what we planned. Noor goes to the supermarket on Thursday after dinner, with a short list, and comes home with exactly what she meant to buy.

One week Noor tries shopping online, because there are no special displays to tempt her. Some people find this easier, though saved favourites can make it just as easy to reorder snacks, so a list still helps.
Idris suggests that Noor keeps big packets of treats out of the house, and buys a small treat when she really wants one. Then having a treat becomes a decision and not an accident.

Hana visits on Sunday and says that the kitchen looks like a different flat. Noor's notebook shows fewer late-night entries now, though there are still some, and Idris says that is how change usually looks.
Noor digs out an old magazine diet and shows it to Idris. She tells him that it went well for ten days, and then she ate everything in sight for a week.

Strict rules can make a forbidden food seem bigger in the mind. When people try hard not to think about a food, they often end up thinking about it even more.

A week has about twenty-one meals, if we count three a day, and a biscuit is a very small part of that. One biscuit does not ruin a week, and it does not change who you are.

Research suggests that people with a flexible approach, who allow themselves some treats, often do better in the long run than people with rigid rules. They also tend to feel out of control less often.
Idris teaches her what he calls the next-meal rule for a bad day. After a slip, she does not wait until Monday to start again, but simply makes the next meal a good one.

Noor thinks about her own street for a long moment today. It has a fast-food shop and a small corner store, and the supermarket is fifteen minutes away by bus.

Idris shares a few budget tips that are useful for anyone. Compare the price per kilo, try the shop's own brand, and plan meals so that less food is wasted.
Idris shows Noor how to make a quick meal in a single pan. Eggs, spinach and tomatoes take about ten minutes, and there is only one pan to wash afterwards.
On Sunday afternoon Noor cooks a big pot of lentil stew and freezes it in single portions. After that, on a tired evening, a good dinner is already waiting in the freezer.
Idris admits that for some people the problem is not knowledge or willpower but simply money. He says that this is not a personal failure, and that help exists for those who struggle to afford food.
Noor's Auntie Leila invites her to a big family lunch on Sunday. Noor is happy to go, but she worries that she will not be able to stick to her new habits.
Idris reminds her that food is also love and belonging. In many families, feeding people is how care is shown, so refusing food can feel like refusing the person.
At Auntie Leila's table there are far too many dishes, and every plate is passed to Noor with a happy cry of eat, eat. She feels torn between her plan and her aunt.
Idris gives her a few tips for the lunch. Take a smaller first plate, praise the cook warmly, and ask to take some leftovers home for tomorrow.
Idris says that family traditions matter and that nobody needs to give them up. Small changes, such as more beans and vegetables in a dish, can keep all the flavours that people love.

Social pressure shows up in many places, such as birthday cakes at the office and friends who say, go on, just one. Idris says that Noor can answer with a happy yes, or with a friendly no thank you, and she owes nobody an explanation.
Idris points out that food companies spend large sums on advertising, and a lot of it is aimed at children. Studies in several countries suggest that this advertising works.
For one day Noor counts the food adverts that she sees on buses, phones and shop windows. She loses count at forty, and she notices that most of them show snacks, sweets or fast food.
Noor's younger brother Sami says that his small daughter Yara begs for the cereal with the cartoon tiger on the box. Idris explains that children are especially open to this kind of persuasion.
At the lunch Noor takes a small first plate, praises the stew and eats a second helping of vegetables. She takes leftovers home, and Auntie Leila beams with joy, so it is the best meal in weeks.
Sami brings Yara for tea, and she pushes away the broccoli, as she does every time. Idris tells him that children often need to try a new food many times before they like it.
Idris suggests offering just a small piece without any pressure or bribes. Children also learn from watching other people enjoy the food, so it helps if the grown-ups eat it too.
Noor admits that she hated cabbage as a child, and she still avoids it today. Idris tells her that the tastes of adults can change too, and that nothing about taste is fixed forever.
Many people find that after they cut down on sugar for a few weeks, sweet things taste sweeter than before. Noor tries it, and she slowly reduces the sugar in her tea.
Salt works in a similar way, because our taste for it adapts over a few weeks. Herbs, spices, lemon and garlic can fill the gap while the tongue gets used to less.
Idris insists that healthy food must taste good, or nobody will eat it. He roasts carrots and cauliflower with a little oil and cumin, and the edges go brown and sweet, so even Noor asks for more.
Idris also has a few useful tricks for bitter greens at home. A little salt, some olive oil, a squeeze of lemon or a spell in a hot oven can all soften the bitterness.
Idris reminds her that adding a healthy food is easier than banning a favourite one. Noor starts by stirring a handful of spinach into her eggs, and she hardly notices it is there.
Noor and Hana decide to try one new food each week, and they keep a list. Some are a success and some are not, and both kinds of result teach them something about their own taste.
On about the ninth try, Yara eats a small piece of broccoli without any fuss. Sami remembers Idris's advice and says nothing at all, and he only smiles at his plate.
Idris asks Noor to draw a timeline of her eating on a normal day. She sees that she skips breakfast and eats a small lunch, and all the hunger comes crashing down in the evening.
For many people, skipping meals leads to a huge hunger in the evening. A filling breakfast and regular meals can keep it manageable, though people differ and some do well with a later first meal.
Noor makes a list of easy breakfasts that she actually likes. Porridge, eggs, yoghurt with fruit, or wholemeal toast with beans are all quick, and they keep her full until lunch.
Lunch is no longer a sad little salad for Noor. She takes a box of leftover stew to work, and the protein and fibre keep her going through the long afternoon.
Idris suggests a planned snack in the late afternoon, such as fruit and nuts or a small pot of yoghurt. It stops the hunger from building up all the way to the evening.
Eating more slowly gives the fullness signals more time to arrive. Noor tries putting her fork down between bites, and she tries to make a meal last as long as a cup of tea.
Idris gives Noor a single raisin and asks her to eat it as slowly as she can. She notices the smell, the texture and the sweetness, and she finds that one raisin can be a surprisingly big experience.
For some people, thirst can feel a little like hunger. Idris says that a glass of water is a cheap thing to try, and if she is still hungry soon after, she should eat.
Idris says that alcohol can lower our caution, and that it often goes with salty snacks in the evening. It is not forbidden, but it is worth noticing in the notebook.

Noor's new rhythm is breakfast, lunch, a snack and dinner, and the late-night hunger comes much less often. Idris says that rhythms differ, for night workers or people who fast for their faith, and the plan can always bend.
Planning a few easy dinners for the week removes many tiring decisions. On Sunday Noor writes five dinners on a planner and sticks it to the fridge.
Noor turns the planner into a shopping list for the week. She chooses meals that share ingredients, so one bag of vegetables is used in several dinners and nothing is thrown away.
Idris tells her to keep an emergency dinner kit for the evenings when the plan falls apart. Eggs, tinned beans, pasta and frozen vegetables can become a meal in fifteen minutes.
Idris says that treats are not forbidden at all. They are better when they are enjoyed slowly and on purpose, such as a square of good chocolate at the table with tea.
Idris gives her a few tips for enjoying a treat. Sit down, give it your full attention, eat the best part first and stop when it feels like enough.
Eating out is a normal part of life, and Idris does not want Noor to avoid it. She can look at the menu in advance, share a dish with a friend or take half home, and then simply enjoy the evening.
Noor goes away for a week to Hana's family wedding, where the food is wonderful and it is everywhere. She eats freely, enjoys every dish and does not feel guilty at all.
A week later Noor catches a cold and has no energy to cook. She lets the plan pause and eats soup and toast, because illness is not the time for rules.
After the wedding and the cold, her fridge is almost empty and her habits feel rusty. Noor restarts with one small step, planning one good meal and not the whole week.
Idris and Noor read the notebook together and sort what works from what does not. The plan should fit her life, he says, and it should bend without breaking.
Hana starts a fashionable diet that she found online, and she is delighted with it. Noor wonders whether she should copy her friend and drop her own slow, careful plan.
Idris says that bodies differ because of genes, age, sleep, medicines and the tiny living things in the gut. Studies show that people can respond quite differently even to the very same meal.
This means that what works for a friend may not work for you. Noor's notebook, Idris says, is exactly the right tool for finding out what works for her own body.
For any new food claim, Idris suggests four questions. Who benefits from it, what is the evidence, is it extreme, and could you keep it up for years?
Idris says that the best plan is usually the one you can keep. Many different ways of eating can be healthy, he says, if they suit you and you can stay with them.
Eating good food matters for health in itself, whatever the number on the scale says. Noor decides to focus on her habits, her energy and her mood, and she puts the scale at the back of a cupboard.
Idris says that moving your body is good for health and mood, but it should never be a punishment for eating. Noor and Hana start a Saturday walk by the river just because they enjoy it.
Idris says that shame tends to backfire, while kindness towards yourself supports lasting change. Studies suggest that people who are kind to themselves after a slip tend to recover faster.
Idris reminds her that online pictures are edited, chosen and lit to look perfect. Noor stops following the accounts that make her feel small, and she feels lighter right away.
One evening Noor writes a short note to the woman she was at the fridge on that first night. It says that she was not weak, and that she simply did not know yet.
Idris speaks gently about something much more serious now. If eating feels out of control, or very restricted, or brings constant worry, a doctor can help, so asking is wise.
Some people need advice made just for them, such as people with a medical condition, an allergy or a pregnancy. Parents who worry about a child's eating can ask a doctor or a registered dietitian.
Idris smiles and admits that, in his first year of retirement, he sometimes ate chocolate at midnight. Even a dietitian is human, he says, and Noor laughs with relief.
Noor puts the first week of her notebook beside the latest one. The late-night entries have gone from most nights to only one or two, and the later ones are shorter and kinder.
Noor writes down the small changes that work for her: planned dinners, fruit in sight, filling food, enough sleep and kindness. None of them is dramatic, but together they have changed her evenings.
Sami brings Yara to visit, and Noor shows her how to toss carrots in oil and spice before they go into the oven. Yara eats them hot from the tray, and nobody gives a single lecture.
Hana gets tired of her strict diet and asks Noor how she changed her evenings. Noor gives her a small notebook and a pencil, just as Idris once did for her.
Twelve weeks after that first night, Noor stands at the open fridge at ten o'clock again. The old craving comes, she names it as tired, makes a cup of tea and goes to bed without a fight.
Idris tells Noor that eating well is hard because an old appetite lives in a modern food world. Small steps repeated with patience, he says, almost always work better than one heroic effort.

This book has given general information about why healthy eating feels hard, and science is still learning more. It is not medical advice, so please talk to a doctor or a dietitian about your own health.
C1C2: Noor had promised herself a salad for dinner, a sensible plan made with great confidence that very morning. Yet here she stood at ten o'clock at night, lit by the open fridge, thinking only about the biscuits in the cupboard. It was the same story every week, and she had begun to suspect that the fault lay somewhere deep in her own character.

At her desk the next morning, Noor opened a note on her phone that she had once named, with some optimism, Fresh Starts. It held a week of salads, a sugar-free January and a magazine diet with a cheerful name, and each of them had collapsed within a fortnight. Reading the list in the grey office light, she felt less like a woman with a plan and more like a woman with a pattern.

It occurred to Noor, somewhere between the third and fourth failed plans on her list, that her uncle Idris had spent forty years as a dietitian. At lunchtime she stood by a window in the corridor and phoned him, feeling oddly embarrassed, as though she were confessing to a crime. Idris listened for a moment and then said, quite simply, that he would come on Saturday and bring the tea.

On Saturday afternoon Idris appeared at her door with a paper bag of oranges in one hand and a battered tin of tea in the other. He settled himself at her small kitchen table, made her sit down opposite him, and then did something that Noor had not expected: he simply listened. She talked for nearly half an hour, and he did not once glance at the biscuit tin on the shelf.

When Noor had finished, Idris stirred his tea and told her, very kindly, that her appetite was no character flaw at all. It was, he said, a very old piece of machinery, built for a different world and doing exactly the job it was built to do. Understanding it, he added, would help her far more than blaming herself ever had.

Idris described his forty years in hospitals and small clinics, where thousands of people had sat in a chair much like hers and described much the same struggle. Almost every one of them had known perfectly well which foods were good for them, and that knowledge had changed remarkably little. The real difficulty, he had come to believe, lay not in knowing what to eat but in everything that surrounds the moment of eating.

Noor objected that she already knew what a healthy dinner looked like, and that she could cook one perfectly well on a good day. Idris nodded, as though she had just made his argument for him, and observed that knowing and doing are two quite separate skills. Between the plan made at breakfast and the fridge opened at night, he said, there is a whole landscape of hunger, habit and tiredness that nobody ever teaches us to cross.

Idris made her a promise at that kitchen table: there would be no scolding, no forbidden lists and no diet sheet covered in small print. Instead they would work like two detectives on a quiet case, asking when the wanting arrived, what had come just before it and how Noor had been feeling at the time. Curiosity, he told her, is a far better tool than shame, and it does not run out by Wednesday.

Before he left, Idris pressed a small green notebook and a pencil into her hands. She was not to count calories, weigh anything or give herself marks out of ten, he warned; she was merely to write down the time, the place and the feeling whenever a craving arrived. It would be a diary of evidence rather than a diary of guilt, and he thought she might be surprised by what it showed.

That evening the old craving arrived on schedule, and Noor ate her biscuit standing at the counter, exactly as she always did. The difference was that she then picked up the notebook and wrote down the time, the tiredness and the long, grey day behind it. For the first time in months she went to bed feeling curious rather than ashamed, and curiosity, she discovered, makes a surprisingly comfortable pillow.

A week later Idris returned, and Noor handed him the little green notebook with some nervousness, as though it were homework. He read it, nodded, and then began his explanation from a surprising place, far back in time, in a world with no shops, no fridges and no certainty of a meal tomorrow. Everything about her appetite, he promised, would make a good deal more sense from that distant starting point.

For most of human history, our ancestors spent long and tiring days searching for berries, roots, nuts and meat. A good day brought a feast, a bad day brought almost nothing, and hunger was an ordinary companion rather than a rare event. In that kind of life, a body that noticed food quickly and ate well when it could was better prepared than one that did not.

Many scientists believe that in such a world the bodies which enjoyed rich food and stored the spare energy as fat were the ones best placed to survive a lean season. Those who came through hard winters had more chances to raise children, and so their traits were passed on. We are, in a sense, the descendants of people who were rather good at eating when food was there.

Remarkably, newborn babies respond to a drop of something sweet with what looks like pleasure, long before they have learned anything about food. Researchers think this is no accident, because in nature a sweet taste usually points to ripe fruit and ripe fruit is a reliable source of energy. A liking for sweetness, in other words, arrives with us rather than being learned from a biscuit tin.

Bitterness is another matter, for in the wild a bitter taste can warn that a plant contains something harmful, and a cautious dislike was therefore a sensible protection. This may help to explain why so many children screw up their faces at certain leafy greens, and why some adults never quite warm to them. Many healthy vegetables, it turns out, start with a small handicap that has nothing to do with willpower.

We are also drawn to fat and to salt, and the reasons are much the same. Fat is a dense store of energy, the body needs a little salt to work properly, and for many of our ancestors both were precious, scattered and difficult to find. A body that gave a small reward for finding them was simply doing its best to keep us supplied.

Honey was a rare and sometimes painful prize, since bees do not surrender it willingly, and for a long time sweetness had to be searched for. Sugar itself was an expensive luxury in much of Europe for centuries, and it became cheap and ordinary only in the last couple of hundred years or so. That is a very short time indeed, when set beside the long story of the human body.

Today Noor can buy something sweet, fatty and salty on almost every corner, at any hour, for the price of a few coins and a short walk. An appetite designed in a world of scarcity now lives in a world of abundance, and the two have never quite learned to get along. Idris compared it to old software running on a new machine: it works hard, but it was never written for this.

Idris was careful to add that scientists still argue about many of the details, and that nobody can prove exactly how each of our tastes first arose. The story of scarcity is a useful way of thinking about appetite, he said, but it should be held loosely, as a good explanation rather than a final truth. Noor liked it very much that he was honest about what was still uncertain, and she trusted him all the more for it.

Looking back through the notebook, Noor noticed that nearly all her cravings clustered in the tired hours after work, while lunchtime passed with hardly a ripple. Idris tapped the page and said that this pattern was worth far more than any list of rules, and that the next step was to look at what happens inside the body when hunger rises. Noor, to her own considerable surprise, found that she was looking forward to the next lesson.

Idris pulled a paper napkin across the table and sketched a stomach, a brain and a wobbling line joining the two. Hunger, he explained, is not a mood that descends from nowhere but a message, carried by nerves and chemicals, between the body that needs fuel and the brain that must decide what to do about it. Once she thought of it as a conversation, Noor found it far less mysterious.

One of the key messengers, Idris said, is a hormone called ghrelin, produced mainly in the lining of the stomach. Its level climbs as a meal grows overdue, nudging the brain to look for food, and it falls away again once we have eaten. Some people call it the hunger hormone, which is a slight simplification, but it is a useful picture to carry in the mind.

Ghrelin appears to follow routine as well, for people who eat at regular times often find that their hunger turns up punctually, just before the habitual meal. The body, it seems, learns the timetable of the day and prepares for lunch the way a dog prepares for a walk when it hears the lead being lifted. Idris stressed that this learning is flexible, and that a new timetable can be taught.

Noor checked the notebook and was startled to see how reliable her hunger was, rumbling at about one o'clock and again at about four, day after day. She had always thought of her appetite as moody and unpredictable, a creature that attacked without warning. It was beginning to look more like a well-trained employee who simply reported for duty at the usual hours.

After we eat, the stomach stretches to hold the food, and the gut begins sending signals to the brain, carried by nerves and by a number of hormones, that say we have had enough. No single messenger is in charge, and the whole system resembles a busy committee rather than a switch. Fullness, Idris reminded her, is something the body announces rather than something we decide.

The fullness signals, Idris went on, do not arrive instantly, and it takes a while for them to build up and reach the brain.
