A fast eater can therefore finish a large portion before the message has even been delivered, rather like a letter that arrives after the person it was meant for has already left. Exact timings vary from person to person, so he preferred not to quote a magic number.

Alongside these short-term messages, Idris said, the body keeps a slower and longer record of its energy reserves, and a hormone called leptin plays a large part in it. Leptin is made by fat tissue and carried in the blood to the brain, where it helps to report how much stored energy the body is holding. It is less like a dinner bell that rings before a meal and more like a bank statement that arrives once in a while.

Idris warned Noor not to take his tidy diagram too literally, since ghrelin and leptin are only two voices in a very crowded conversation. Scientists have found many other hormones, nerve signals and chemicals that take part, and they are still learning how all of them fit together. The system is not a pair of switches that can be flipped, but a sprawling network that has been refined over a very long time.

Appetite, Idris said, is much like thirst, in that it is a real need of the body and not a matter of opinion. You may be able to ignore it for a while with a great effort of will, but you cannot argue it out of existence, and the longer you ignore it the louder it becomes. Telling yourself not to be hungry is a little like telling yourself not to be thirsty after a long walk in the sun.

Idris then drew a distinction that Noor had never thought about: hunger is the body asking for fuel, whereas appetite is a wish for a particular food, and the two do not always arrive together. She looked at the notebook and realised that on most of her late evenings she had eaten a perfectly good dinner not long before, which meant that the biscuits were not answering hunger at all. Something else was calling her, and she was determined to find out exactly what it was.

Whenever we eat something delicious, Idris explained, the brain's reward system quietly makes a note of the experience, filing it under things worth repeating. The next time we meet that food, or anything connected with it, the brain nudges us towards it before we have had time to think. It is a learning system, and it learns quickly, which is a great advantage when food is scarce and rather a nuisance when it is not.

Researchers who study the brain distinguish carefully between wanting something and liking it, and they believe a chemical messenger called dopamine is involved in the first more than the second. Noor recognised this at once, for by the fourth biscuit she was still reaching into the packet, though she could scarcely taste it any more. Wanting, it seemed, can keep running long after the pleasure has quietly gone home for the night.

Idris pointed out that cues such as smells, sights, sounds and adverts can set the wanting going before we have made any decision at all. The scent of baking bread drifting from a doorway is the classic example, but a glossy photograph of a burger can do the same job from the other side of a screen. By the time we notice that we want something, the process has usually been under way for several seconds.

Reading back through the notebook, Noor found a pattern that she had never seen from the inside. On the long, tiring days she nearly always bought a pastry from the bakery on Mill Street, the one she passed on her walk home, while on easy days she walked straight by. The craving, it seemed, depended on the day and the doorway as much as on the pastry.

Idris explained that the place, the hour and the mood are all part of the cue, because the brain links everything that surrounds a reward with the reward itself. After many tired walks home past the same shop window, the whole scene had become a signal, and the wanting began as soon as the door came into view. It was not a failure of character but a very efficient piece of learning.

Idris proposed an experiment, careful to say that it was not a punishment and not a rule for life. For three days Noor took a different route home, past a quiet park instead of the bakery, and recorded in the notebook exactly what she felt at each stage of the walk. She thought it a rather odd thing for a grown woman to be doing, yet she found herself oddly curious about the result.

On the first evening the wanting was strong, and she very nearly turned round to retrace her steps. By the third day, however, it had weakened noticeably, as though the cue had lost some of its hold, although the biscuits at home still called to her in the usual way. Idris was pleased with this mixed result, since changing one cue rarely solves everything and an honest experiment should say so.

Noor then noticed that her phone had become a cue machine, offering a sizzling food video at eight, a discount for takeaway pizza at nine and a cheerful notification from the delivery app just when she was most tired. None of it was an accident, for these messages are timed and designed to catch people exactly when the wanting is easiest to wake. She turned off the notifications that very night and felt, to her surprise, a small but definite relief.

Idris compared a craving to a wave on the sea, which rises, reaches its crest and then fades away, whether or not anyone does anything about it. Many people find that the strongest part passes within a short time if they can simply watch it without obeying it, although he admitted that this varies from person to person and from craving to craving. It is not a magic trick, he said, but it is a skill that improves with practice.

The next time the craving arrived, Noor set a kitchen timer for ten minutes, made herself a cup of tea and sat down to watch the wave rise. On some evenings the craving faded before the timer rang, and on others she ate her biscuit with great enjoyment, and Idris insisted that both outcomes were useful. Either way she had gathered one more piece of evidence, and she had done it without a single harsh word to herself.

Idris set a plain loaf of bread beside a brightly coloured snack packet and asked Noor what she saw. The words he wanted were ultra-processed, a term some researchers use for foods made in factories from long lists of ingredients, many of which you would never find in a home kitchen. The packet, with its crisp wrapper and its cheerful promises, was a perfect example.

Idris was quick to add that processing is not a dirty word, since freezing peas, tinning tomatoes, cooking beans and baking bread are all forms of it, and many are useful. The concern is with the far end of the scale, where foods are built from industrial ingredients rather than prepared from ordinary ones, and experts still argue about exactly where the lines should fall. He asked Noor to remember that it is a spectrum, not a single villain.

Many ultra-processed foods are designed with great care to be as appealing as possible, and the companies that make them test the sweetness, the saltiness and the crunch again and again on panels of tasters. The aim is a product that delights at the first bite and invites a second and a third, which is excellent business and rather less good for a person with a biscuit tin. Noor felt faintly flattered and faintly insulted to learn how much cleverness had gone into her weakness.

Texture matters too, and many of these foods are soft, crisp or crumbly, so that they dissolve in the mouth with almost no chewing. That makes them quick to eat, and quick eating, as Noor had already learned, leaves the body's fullness signals trailing far behind. A bag of crisps can disappear in the time it takes a carrot to be properly chewed.

In one careful study, a small group of adults lived at a research centre and ate two different diets in turn, each for two weeks. The meals were matched to look similar in their sugar, fat and fibre, and the volunteers were free to eat as much as they liked, yet on the ultra-processed diet they took in about five hundred more calories a day. It was a small study, Idris stressed, but it was unusually well controlled, and it has made many scientists curious.

Scientists are still debating why the volunteers ate so much more, and no single explanation has been proved. Faster eating, soft textures and foods that pack a great deal of energy into a small bite may all play a part, and it is also possible that other features of the food are involved. Idris liked this honesty in science, and he asked Noor to be wary of anyone who claims to know the one true cause.

Variety, Idris noted, is another quiet driver of appetite, for the body grows tired of one flavour but responds to a new one with fresh interest. That is why a party table crowded with different snacks is so easy to keep returning to, and why most of us still find room for pudding after a large meal. Appetite for a single taste fades, but appetite for novelty is remarkably hard to exhaust.

Back at the flat, Noor opened her cupboard and counted six half-finished packets of biscuits, crisps and chocolate, each one a different flavour and texture. Without ever meaning to, she had built herself a small buffet, and every time she tired of one taste another was waiting. Plain foods, by contrast, such as boiled rice or an apple, bored her quickly, which made them easy to stop eating and rather hard to overeat.

Idris warned her that words on the front of a packet, such as natural, light or high in protein, tell you what the marketing department wants you to notice rather than what the food really is. A short list of ordinary ingredients on the back is a rough guide, he said, though it is only a guide and certainly no reason to panic about every packet in the supermarket. Perfection, he reminded her with a smile, was never part of the plan, and a few packets would never ruin anything.

Noor sat back and realised that she had not been weak at all, because she had been facing foods designed by clever people to be easy to eat and hard to stop. Idris said that the calm answer was neither a ban nor a war, only a gentle drift towards more whole foods on most days, with room left over for everything else. It was the first piece of advice all week that did not make her feel like a patient.

On his next visit Idris arrived with a bag of red lentils, borrowed Noor's biggest saucepan and began to make soup while he talked. Some foods, he explained, fill us up far more than others even when they hold exactly the same energy, which is why some meals leave us satisfied and others leave us hunting through the cupboards. The soup, bubbling gently on the stove, was to be his first exhibit in the case.

The first reason that lentils fill us up, Idris said, is fibre, the part of plants that the body cannot fully digest. It adds bulk to the meal and slows the passage of food, so the feeling of fullness lasts longer, and it is found in beans, oats, vegetables, fruit and whole grains. Noor had always thought of fibre as boring, but she was starting to see that boring and filling often go together.

The second reason, he continued, is protein, which in many studies appears to satisfy hunger better than the same amount of energy from other nutrients. It is found in eggs, fish, beans, lentils, meat and dairy foods, and a meal built around it tends to keep the stomach quiet for longer. Idris added that bodies differ and the evidence is not perfectly tidy, but the general pattern has been seen many times.

The third reason is simply water, for soups, stews, fruit and vegetables are full of it, and water adds volume without adding energy. A large bowl of soup therefore fills the stomach in a way that a small piece of pastry, however rich, never quite manages. Idris tasted his own cooking, added a pinch of cumin and remarked that the stomach, unlike the tongue, is rather impressed by size.

Idris peeled an orange and set it beside a glass of orange juice, and he asked her which would fill her more. The whole fruit, with its fibre and its slow chewing, almost certainly would, whereas the juice slips down in a few swallows and leaves the appetite scarcely troubled. Juice is not a crime, he added, but it behaves quite differently from the fruit it came from.

Drinks with sugar in them tend to satisfy us less than solid food does, so their energy is remarkably easy to overlook. Noor looked at her notebook and recalled the large, sweet, creamy coffee she bought every afternoon at about three, a drink that had never once registered in her mind as a snack. It had been sitting in plain sight, quietly doing the work of a small cake.

Idris invited her to run a small experiment of her own, and Noor agreed with some enthusiasm. On one morning she ate a bowl of oat porridge and on the next a bowl of sweet, crunchy cereal, and each time she wrote down in the notebook exactly how hungry she felt at eleven o'clock. She was starting to enjoy being a scientist in her own kitchen, with a spoon for a microscope.

The porridge morning went noticeably better, for Noor stayed satisfied until lunch, whereas after the cereal she was searching her desk drawer by eleven. Idris cautioned that a single test is not proof, since sleep, stress and a dozen other things can tip the result, but it was her own evidence and it pointed in a sensible direction. He told her to repeat it a few times before she trusted it fully.

Idris introduced the idea of energy density, which simply means how much energy is packed into each mouthful of food. Vegetables and soups sit at the low end, while pastry, oil and chocolate sit at the high end, and the body does not always notice the difference. He was careful to say that dense foods are not wicked, since nuts and olive oil are good for most people, and that the point was merely to understand why some plates fill us more cheaply than others.

Idris offered her a simple picture for dinner, which was some vegetables, some protein and a starchy food with plenty of fibre, and he insisted that it was a picture rather than a rule. Noor ate the lentil soup with a slice of seeded bread and a small salad, and she noticed afterwards that the evening felt different. The craving still came a little before ten, but it was quieter, and it did not have to shout to be heard.

In the supermarket, Noor lifted a giant packet of crisps that was on special offer, and Idris watched her weigh it in her hand. Experiments in many settings have shown that people tend to eat more when the portion in front of them is larger, and they do so without feeling that they have been greedy. The effect is surprisingly steady, he told her, and it is rather hard to notice from the inside.

The effect has been found with many kinds of food, from snacks at the cinema to main meals at home, and in people of every age. Those who are handed a larger share very often finish a larger share, even when they do not rate the food as any more enjoyable than the smaller helpings. The portion in front of us, it seems, quietly tells us what a normal amount looks like.

Some studies suggest that a large plate makes a portion look smaller, so that we serve ourselves more in order to feel that we have a proper meal. The evidence is mixed, Idris admitted, and the effect is probably modest, but a smaller plate costs nothing and carries no risk. He told Noor to treat it as an experiment rather than a rule, which was, by now, how she treated most things.

When we eat straight from a packet, Idris pointed out, there is no natural stopping place, and the bottom of the bag arrives as a shock. Noor tried pouring a modest portion into a small bowl instead, and was struck by how clearly she felt the moment when it was finished. It was not a dramatic victory, but it turned a blur into a decision, which is a smaller and a better thing.

Portions in restaurants and takeaways are often generous, and many people believe that standard sizes have grown steadily over the last few decades. Most of us, faced with a heaped plate, feel a quiet obligation to finish it, as though leaving food were somehow impolite to the chef. Idris said that this feeling is natural and perfectly harmless, but that it does not always match what our bodies actually need.

Many of us were taught as children to clear our plates, often with good reasons, since food costs money and wasting it feels wrong. Yet the habit can train us to override the body's signal that we have had enough, and Idris suggested a gentler rule: serve a little less, and take more if you are still hungry. Leftovers, he reminded her, are simply tomorrow's lunch with a helpful head start in the morning.

Noor often ate her dinner at her desk, one eye on a screen and the other on her fork, hardly looking at either. Idris explained that eating while distracted can lead people to eat more at the time, and in some studies to eat more again later, because the meal leaves such a faint memory. A meal we do not notice, he said, is a meal the brain has not quite counted.

Noor laughed in recognition, because her notebook was full of evenings on which she had looked down from a screen and found, to her astonishment, that a whole bowl of crisps had vanished. She could not recall tasting a single one, and the empty bowl seemed to belong to somebody else. It was both funny and slightly sad that something she wanted so much had left no trace in her memory.

Idris added that people often eat more in company than alone, lingering over a meal, taking second helpings and matching the pace of those around them. This is not a fault, for sharing food is one of the oldest human pleasures, but it does mean that the people at the table shape what we eat as much as the food on it. He saw no reason to give up a good dinner with friends, only to notice it.

For a week, Noor tried eating her dinner at the small table, with the laptop shut and her phone turned face down beside the salt. Her meals took longer, the food tasted better than she remembered, and she felt pleasantly full by the end, although on two nights she forgot and found herself back at the desk with a fork in the air. Idris said that two out of seven was a very respectable start, and that a habit is built from such uneven beginnings.

One grey morning Noor yawned three times before she had even finished her first cup of coffee, and Idris, who had come early to deliver a bag of oranges, noticed every one of them. He asked her, quite gently, how she had been sleeping lately, and she hesitated before she answered. She admitted that she went to bed late three or four nights a week and often woke before the alarm.

When volunteers in sleep experiments are allowed too few hours in bed, Idris told her, they often report feeling hungrier the next day, and they tend to reach for richer, sweeter food. Some studies have also found changes in the hormones that manage hunger and fullness, with ghrelin tending to rise and leptin to fall. The research is not perfectly consistent, but the general direction has turned up again and again.

Noor went through her notebook for the last month and drew a small moon beside every day that followed a poor night. The pattern was clear enough to be embarrassing, for her fiercest cravings came almost always after her shortest nights, and her gentlest evenings after the nights when she had slept well. She had been blaming her willpower for something that her pillow was largely responsible for.

Some brain scanning studies suggest that people who are short of sleep respond more strongly to pictures of tempting food, as though the reward system had turned up its volume. At the same time the parts of the mind responsible for planning and restraint seem to work less smoothly, so the cake is louder and the voice of caution is quieter. Idris cautioned that these studies are small, but they matched what he had seen in many tired patients.

When we are tired, Idris observed, we naturally look for quick energy, and the nearest sources are usually sugar and caffeine. A coffee late in the afternoon can linger in the body for many hours and make the next night's sleep shallower, which in turn makes the next day's cravings stronger. It is a quiet loop, and like most loops it can be broken at more than one point.

Bright screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep, and the endless scrolling keeps the mind busy long after the body is ready to rest. Noor admitted, with a small wince, that she often lay in bed with her phone for an hour after she had meant to sleep, moving from one clip to the next without really enjoying any of them. Idris did not scold her; he asked what she thought she was hoping to find there.

For some people, Idris said, a large meal eaten very late can make it harder to sleep comfortably, although others notice no difference at all. Late-night eating also tends to mean snacking in front of a screen, which brings back everything Noor had learned about distraction and cues in a single evening. The simplest remedy was not a rule about the clock, but a calm and satisfying dinner at a sensible hour.

Idris shared a few simple sleep basics which many people find useful, such as keeping similar bedtimes, making the bedroom dark and cool, and leaving the coffee for the morning. He was careful to say that this was general advice and not a treatment, and that anyone who has trouble sleeping for a long time should speak to a doctor. Noor noticed with some relief that none of his suggestions involved giving up anything she loved.

Idris remembered the night-shift workers he used to see in the clinic, among them nurses, bus drivers and bakers, whose body clocks were permanently out of step with the rest of the world. Researchers believe that eating at odd hours can make appetite and digestion harder to manage, and he had never once met a night worker who was lazy. They needed kindness and a good plan, he said, far more than they needed a lecture.

For a week, Noor switched off her lamp by eleven, with her phone plugged in on the far side of the room where it could not tempt her. The cravings did not vanish, and she still had one evening when the biscuit tin won, but they were noticeably quieter, and her mornings felt less like climbing a wall. Idris was careful to say that sleep is no cure-all, though he looked quietly delighted.

It was deadline week at the office, and Noor stayed late every evening, frowning at spreadsheets under a flickering light. Her colleague Hana kept a large jar of sweets on her desk, and Noor found herself dipping into it every hour or so without ever making a decision to do it. By Thursday the notebook was full of small, anxious entries, and the jar was nearly empty.

Idris read the anxious little entries carefully and told her that stress changes appetite in ways that differ from person to person. Many people find that they want more comfort food when they are under pressure, and some researchers link this to the body's stress hormones, while others lose their appetite altogether and forget to eat. Neither response was a flaw, he said; both were the body trying to cope.

Rich, sweet and fatty foods can feel genuinely soothing in the moment, which is exactly why we call them comfort food, and the relief they offer is real rather than imagined. The difficulty is that the relief is short, and it fades much faster than the worry that called for it. Idris saw no shame in reaching for comfort; he wanted only to make sure that Noor had more than one way to find it.

Many of us, Idris pointed out, learned in childhood to link food with feeling better, through the sweet after a fall, the treat for being brave or the biscuit that arrived with a hug. Noor remembered her mother's sweet tea and a plate of biscuits on every difficult evening of her school years, and she felt a rush of affection at the thought. The link was not a weakness at all, but a lasting trace of being loved.

Idris explained that physical hunger usually builds slowly and would be satisfied by almost any decent meal, whereas hunger driven by feeling tends to arrive suddenly and to insist on one particular food. It often leaves a vague dissatisfaction even when the plate is empty, since what was really wanted was never on the plate. The difference is not always clear, he cautioned, and nobody should be expected to tell them apart perfectly.

Before she reached for a snack, Noor tried pausing for a few seconds to name the feeling underneath, whether it was tiredness, loneliness, irritation or plain boredom. Psychologists have found that putting a name to an emotion often takes some of the pressure out of it, though the effect is modest and does not work for everyone every time. She was surprised how often the answer was simply tired, and how rarely it was hungry.

Idris suggested that Noor write a short menu of comforts that did not involve the kitchen, to sit beside food rather than replace it. A walk round the block, a favourite song, a warm shower or a telephone call to a friend were all on the list, and she pinned it inside a cupboard door. A person with only one comfort, he said, will lean on it far too hard.

When Noor confided in Hana about the notebook and the cravings, Hana burst out laughing and confessed that she kept a chocolate emergency in her bottom drawer. Having found a fellow sufferer, the two of them agreed to take a ten-minute walk each afternoon, with no rule against buying a coffee at the end of it. Nothing about the plan was dramatic, and that, Noor decided, was exactly what made it work.

Idris was firm that comfort eating is a normal human thing, and that a biscuit with a cup of tea on a hard evening is nothing to be ashamed of. It becomes a concern only when food is the single tool a person has for every difficult feeling, or when the eating itself leaves them distressed, frightened or out of control. In that case, he said, there is real help available, and asking for it is a sign of sense rather than failure.

On her next bad day, Noor sat down with a cup of tea and a single biscuit, which she ate slowly, noticing the sweetness and the crumbly edge as though she were tasting it for the first time. Then she put on her shoes and walked around the block while the streetlights came on one by one. That night she wrote in the notebook just three words, I was kind, and she underlined them twice.

Idris drew a neat circle with three arrows and labelled them in turn: trigger, action and payoff. A habit, he explained, is simply a loop of that kind which has been repeated so many times that the brain no longer needs to think about it, and runs it automatically. Noor stared at the little diagram and had the uncomfortable feeling that she was looking at a map of her own evenings.

Noor took the pencil and drew her own loop beneath his, writing the words slowly as she went. The trigger was a tired walk home, the action was a warm pastry from the bakery on Mill Street, and the payoff was a few precious minutes of relief and sweetness at the end of a long day. Seeing it laid out so plainly, she stopped feeling guilty and began to feel interested.

The brain, Idris said, is a great saver of effort, and it turns repeated actions into automatic routines so that we can spare our attention for new things. It is rather like driving home along a road you know so well that you arrive without remembering a single junction. Automatic habits are not a defect of the mind but one of its most useful tricks, and the trouble comes only when the habit does not serve us.

Old habits, Idris warned, rarely disappear completely, and the old loop probably remains in the brain long after we have stopped using it. It is therefore usually easier to build a new path beside it than to try to erase the old one, much as a worn track across a lawn fades only when a better route is laid. Noor found this oddly comforting, since it meant that a slip was not a defeat but simply the old track being walked on.

Idris suggested that Noor keep the trigger and the payoff and change only the action in the middle of the loop. The tired walk would remain, and so would the few minutes of relief, but the pastry would be replaced by a flask of hot tea drunk on a bench in the park. It would not be exactly the same reward, he admitted, yet it would answer the same need, which is why such swaps tend to last.

Noor wrote a short plan on a card in the form that psychologists call an if-then plan: if I feel the pull at the bakery door, then I walk on to the bench in the park. Research suggests that specific plans of this kind help people to follow through, because the decision has already been made in a calm moment, long before the tired one. She slipped the card into her coat pocket like a small, hopeful ticket for the evening journey.

Idris told her that the commonest mistake in changing a habit is to aim too high at the start, for the enthusiasm of a Monday rarely survives a hard Thursday. A new habit should be so small that it feels almost silly, such as adding one piece of fruit to breakfast or drinking a glass of water before dinner. Small habits grow more easily than large ones, he said, and they have a way of attracting company.

In one study of people building new habits, the average time for a habit to feel automatic was about two months, although the range ran from a few weeks to many months. Idris used this to reassure her that slowness was normal and that no one should judge their progress after a fortnight. In that same study, missing a single day made little difference in the long run, and it was the patient return that counted.

Noor hung a calendar beside the fridge and decided to stick a gold star on it for every evening she made it to the park bench. It looked childish, and she did not care, because Idris had explained that a small flash of satisfaction after a new habit helps the brain to remember that it was worth repeating. By the end of the week she had five stars and a strange, private sense of pride.

On the ninth evening, after a quarrel with a client and a missed train, Noor went into the bakery and bought a pastry without even hesitating. She felt the old sting of failure, but she remembered Idris and wrote down exactly what had set off the craving, then ate the pastry on the bench with her tea. The next evening she walked through the park again, and the star went on the calendar as usual.

One evening Noor sighed over a cold cup of tea and announced that what she really needed was more willpower, as if it were something that could be bought in a shop. Idris asked her, with real curiosity, what she thought willpower actually was, and waited. After a long pause she said that it was the ability to choose what you want in the long run over what you want right now.

Idris agreed with her definition and then added the important part: willpower is not the same all day long, and it weakens when we are tired, hungry or stressed. For most working people that means it is thinnest in the evening, which is precisely when they stand in front of the open fridge. Noor laughed out loud, because he had just described, quite exactly, her entire daily timetable from morning until night.

Idris was honest enough to admit that scientists still argue about how willpower works. A famous idea, that self-control is a limited fuel which runs down with use, has been questioned by later studies, and the question is far from settled. What nobody doubts, he added, is that tired, hungry and stressed people find it harder to hold their course, and that is all Noor needed to know.

An ordinary day, Idris pointed out, is crowded with small decisions, from what to wear and what to answer in an email to which meeting to attend and whom to ignore. By evening the mind has made hundreds of choices, and it may have little patience left for the last one, which happens to be whether to open the cupboard. It is not weakness, he said, but simply a very full head at the end of a very long day.

The wise answer, Idris said, is not to demand more of yourself at your weakest hour but to plan when you are strongest. A decision made at breakfast, when the mind is calm and the stomach is full, will do far more than any heroic effort at ten o'clock at night, because it has already been taken. Noor liked the idea of leaving instructions for her tired self, like a kind note from a thoughtful friend.

Some studies of people who are good at self-control give a rather surprising result, for these people are often not heroes of resistance at all. Instead, they tend to arrange their lives so that they meet fewer temptations in the first place, which means they rarely have to fight the same battle twice. The strongest people, Idris concluded, seem to be those who use their strength the least.

Idris summed up the idea in a single sentence: make the healthy choice the easy one, and the unhelpful choice a little harder. A biscuit that takes five more steps to reach is eaten less often than one at arm's length, and a piece of fruit on the counter is eaten far more than the same fruit hidden in a drawer. Friction, he said, is the quiet ally of anyone with a tired mind and a busy week.

Hunger, Idris reminded her, changes not only the stomach but the whole manner of thinking, so that a hungry person sees food as larger, closer and more urgent than a fed one does. It is therefore wise to make decisions about food when you are comfortably full, and to leave the hard choices to a version of yourself who is calm. A shopping trip before lunch, he warned, was a favour to nobody, least of all to your purse.

With Idris's help Noor wrote a short card called the Tired Evening Plan and stuck it to the fridge door where she could not miss it. It said that dinner would be ready by seven, that a cup of tea and a warm shower would follow, and that the cupboard would stay shut until she had done both. She felt slightly foolish writing it, and distinctly relieved every time she read it.

Idris said something that Noor wrote at the top of a fresh page: guilt is not a fuel. Harsh self-criticism, he believed, drains the very energy that change requires, and he had seen it flatten far more people than it had ever lifted. Noor decided on the spot to retire the word weak from her vocabulary, and she crossed it out of the notebook in three firm strokes.

Idris stood in the doorway of Noor's small kitchen and asked her a curious question: what was the first thing her eye landed on when she walked in? What we can see and reach most easily, he explained, is what we tend to eat, so the arrangement of a kitchen matters rather more than its colour. Noor looked round and saw, with some dismay, a large tin of biscuits standing in the very centre of the counter.

In experiments in offices and canteens, Idris said, people tended to eat noticeably more when food was in plain view and within easy reach. They ate noticeably less when the same food was tucked into a drawer or placed across the room, and nobody in these studies was being forbidden anything. It was a humbling reminder that our choices are shaped by the furniture as much as by the mind.

That same afternoon Noor set about rearranging her kitchen with the zeal of a woman redecorating a palace. A bowl of apples and oranges took pride of place in the middle of the counter, and the biscuit tin was carried to the highest cupboard and hidden behind the saucepans. She stepped back to admire the result and thought that the room looked, for once, like it was on her side.

The biscuits were not banned, and Idris was most insistent on that point, for Noor could still reach the tin whenever she wished, provided that she fetched the stool. The effort created a small pause, and in that pause she could ask herself whether she genuinely wanted a biscuit or merely wanted something to happen. On some evenings she fetched the stool, and on others she put the kettle on instead.

The fridge received the same treatment, for Idris pointed out that it, too, was a shop window that Noor visited several times a day. At the front and at eye level she placed chopped carrots, a tub of hummus and boxes of cooked beans, while the leftovers went into clear containers where she could not forget them. Food that is easy to see and ready to eat, he said, has a surprisingly good chance of being eaten.

Idris reminded her that a supermarket is designed, with great skill, to sell goods and not to help anyone plan a week of balanced meals. Special displays at the ends of the aisles, sweets glittering beside the tills and bright offers on the most tempting items are all placed where the eye will fall. A shopper without a plan, he said, is a shopper who has been planned for.

Shopping after a meal, and with a list in hand, helps people to buy what they planned rather than what they pass. On Thursday Noor went to the supermarket straight after dinner with a short list written in pencil, and she walked past the cakes feeling oddly invulnerable. She came home with exactly what she had intended, plus one small bar of chocolate that she had decided on in advance.

One week Noor tried ordering her groceries online, partly because there would be no glittering displays to tempt her on the way to the tills. Idris said that some people find this easier, although a screen has its own tricks, and a list of saved favourites can make it just as simple to order snacks as vegetables. In either case, he said, a plan made calmly beforehand is the real protection.

Idris suggested that Noor avoid keeping large family-size packets of treats in the flat, and buy a single small one when she really wanted it. Having a treat then becomes a decision instead of an accident, and a treat chosen on purpose is usually enjoyed far more than one that simply happens. He added that this was her choice entirely, and that a household with other tastes would need a different plan.

When Hana visited on Sunday afternoon she stopped in the kitchen doorway and declared that it looked like a different flat. The notebook told the same story, with noticeably fewer late-night entries than in the first weeks, although the occasional one remained and Noor did not pretend otherwise. Idris said that this is what real change usually looks like, which is to say gradual, uneven and quietly encouraging.

Noor dug out the old magazine diet from the bottom of a drawer and handed it over with an apologetic smile. She told him that it had gone beautifully for ten days, with tiny meals and a feeling of enormous virtue, and then collapsed into a week in which she seemed to eat everything in sight. Idris did not laugh, because he had heard that same story a thousand times before in his clinic.

Idris explained that very strict diets can backfire, because the body defends itself against weight loss. In studies of people who have lost weight, hunger signals tend to rise and fullness signals tend to fall, so that appetite pushes back harder the more severely the person has cut down. The body, in other words, treats a diet as a famine, and it responds with the instincts of a famine.

The body may also adapt by burning a little less energy than before, as though turning down the lights to save on the bill, and that makes steady weight loss harder. Scientists are still studying how large this effect is and how it differs from one person to another, so Idris refused to give her a number. The principle, however, was clear enough: the body does not cooperate with crash plans.

Strict rules, Idris said, can make a forbidden food loom larger in the mind than it deserves, because the more we try not to think about something, the more it tends to occupy our thoughts. A biscuit that is banned becomes a symbol, and a symbol is much harder to resist than a mere snack. Noor remembered the endless hours she had spent on the magazine diet thinking about nothing but bread.

Many people who lose weight on strict plans regain much of it over the following years, a pattern that researchers have noted in a great number of studies, although some people do keep it off. Idris insisted that this was a sign of how strongly the body pushes back, and certainly not of a weak mind or a faulty character. The failure, if there was one, belonged to the plan far more than to the person.

Idris described a pattern he called all-or-nothing thinking, and he said that researchers have given it a rather splendid name: the what-the-hell effect. After a single slip, the dieter reasons that the day is ruined anyway and therefore she might as well finish the whole packet, so that a small stumble becomes a long fall. Noor winced in recognition, since she could have written the textbook example herself, with illustrations and footnotes.

Idris drew a grid of twenty-one squares on the back of an envelope, one for each main meal in a week, and coloured a single small corner of one square. That, he said, was the true size of one biscuit in the great scheme of eating, and it was not remotely enough to ruin a week, a month or anything else. The mistake lies not in the biscuit but in the story we tell about it afterwards.

Research suggests that people who take a flexible approach to eating, allowing themselves the occasional treat without drama, often manage better in the long run than those who live by rigid rules. They also appear to be less prone to episodes of out-of-control eating, though the studies cannot prove that flexibility is the cause. Idris saw no reason to doubt that kindness and common sense should go together.

Idris taught her the next-meal rule, which is exactly what it sounds like, and which he had recommended to many patients over the years. After a slip, you do not wait for Monday, or the first of the month, or a new year, but make the very next meal a good one. The beauty of the rule is that it leaves no time for the spiral to take hold, and Noor tried it the following morning with a plate of eggs on toast and felt a surprising lightness.

Idris finished with a warning about extreme fasts, detox programmes and any plan that promises to transform your life within a week. Such promises should always be doubted, he said, because the body has its own perfectly good ways of looking after itself, and extreme methods are often costly and short. Anyone with a medical condition, he added, should talk to a doctor before changing the way they eat.

Noor frowned over a grocery receipt and said that healthy food seemed to cost too much and take too long to prepare. Idris agreed that she had a point, because eating well depends on money, on time and on what is sold near where you live, and not only on the person at the table. Advice that ignores those facts, he said, is really advice for somebody else's life, lived somewhere else.

Neighbourhoods, Idris pointed out, differ enormously, and in some of them fast-food restaurants outnumber the shops that sell fresh vegetables by a wide margin. People tend to eat what is near, cheap and quick, and it is unfair to call that a lack of character when it is really a feature of the map. He had seen the same patients choose very differently when they moved to a street with a good greengrocer.

Noor thought about her own street, and she realised that it fitted the pattern rather well. It had a fast-food shop on one corner and a small store selling mostly crisps and fizzy drinks on the other, while the nearest supermarket was a fifteen-minute bus ride away. Idris suggested that on Saturday morning they take the same bus in the opposite direction, to the market.

The Saturday market was a riot of colour and noise, and at the end of one row stood Mrs Farah, a broad, cheerful stallholder behind mountains of onions, bunches of greens and sacks of lentils. She told Noor to buy whatever was in season, since it was usually fresher and cheaper, and she added a free handful of herbs whenever she felt like it. Noor left with a heavy bag and a surprisingly light feeling in her purse.

Idris laid the bag out on her kitchen table and pointed out that many of the most useful foods are also the cheapest. Beans, lentils, oats, eggs, frozen vegetables and tinned fish all cost very little for what they give, and most of them keep for months in a cupboard or a freezer. Nobody, he said, has ever been turned away from a good meal by a bag of lentils.

Frozen and tinned vegetables, Idris told her, are often similar in nutrition to fresh ones, since they are usually packed soon after picking, and they have the great virtue of not rotting in the fridge. Rinsing tinned beans under a tap washes away some of the salt in the liquid, and a bag of frozen peas will wait patiently for months until she is ready. Fresh food is lovely, he added, but it is not the only good food.

Idris shared a few thrifty tips, none of them glamorous but all of them useful. He suggested comparing the price per kilo rather than the price on the packet, trying the supermarket's own brand, cooking simple dishes from scratch and planning the week's meals so that less food ended up in the bin. Noor realised that she had been paying a good deal for the convenience of not thinking.

Idris showed Noor how a healthy meal can be made in a single pan in about ten minutes, with a few eggs, a handful of spinach and a couple of tomatoes cooked together over a medium heat. There was almost nothing to chop and only one dish to wash afterwards, which is, after all, what a tired person at seven in the evening actually needs. It was a revelation to Noor that dinner could be quicker than the delivery.

On Sunday afternoon Noor cooked a very large pot of lentil stew, let it cool, and divided it into single portions which she stacked in the freezer. From then on, a good dinner was waiting for her on even the most exhausted evening, requiring nothing more than a saucepan and a few minutes of warming. She felt, rather absurdly, like a person who had done something for her future self, and she had.

Idris admitted that for some people the problem is not knowledge or willpower but simply money, and that no amount of clever advice will fill an empty purse. This is a matter of wages, prices, shops and time as much as of personal choices, he said, and it is no failure to ask for help. Many communities have food banks, community meals and support services, and he hoped that anybody who needed them would feel free to use them.

A message arrived from Noor's Auntie Leila, inviting her to the big family lunch that took place on the first Sunday of every month. Noor was delighted to be asked, and at the same time slightly alarmed, because her aunt's table was famous across the whole family for its generosity. She wondered how on earth her new habits would survive a lunch in which refusing a second helping was almost a crime.

Idris listened and then reminded her that food has never been only fuel, for it is also love, belonging and memory. In many families, feeding people is the main way in which care is shown, and refusing a dish can feel to the cook like refusing the person who made it. A plan that ignores this, he said, will lose to a plate of aunt's cooking every single time.

At Auntie Leila's table there were far too many dishes for the number of people, and each one was pressed on Noor with a happy cry of eat, eat. She felt torn between the plan that she had made with such care and the beaming face of the woman holding the serving spoon. It was clear which of the two would win if she did nothing at all.

Before the lunch Idris had given her three tips, none of which required an argument. She could take a smaller first helping and enjoy it slowly, praise the cook warmly and truthfully, and ask whether she might carry some leftovers home for the following day. Generous hosts, he said, are usually delighted when their food is loved and are rarely counting how much is actually eaten.

Idris insisted that family traditions are precious and that nobody should feel obliged to abandon them for the sake of a diet. Small adjustments, such as adding more beans or vegetables to a favourite dish, or using a little less oil, can keep the flavours that everyone loves while giving the meal more fibre. The best changes, he thought, are the ones that nobody at the table even notices.

Social pressure turns up in many places, from birthday cake in the office to the friend who says, go on, just one, and Idris said that eating is rarely a private matter. Noor could answer with a cheerful yes when she wanted the cake, or with a friendly no thank you when she did not, and in neither case did she owe anybody a lecture or an explanation. A smile, he said, is a wonderfully complete reply to nearly every offer of food.

Idris pointed out that food companies spend very large sums on advertising, and that a great deal of it is aimed at children, who are the most trusting audience of all. Studies in several countries suggest that this advertising does influence what young people ask for, and in many cases what they end up eating. It is, in other words, a rather uneven match, and she should not blame herself for losing it.

For a single day Noor kept a tally of every food advert she met, on bus shelters, phone screens, shop windows and the sides of vans. She lost count at forty well before lunchtime, and she noticed with some surprise that very few of them showed vegetables, beans or anything that had to be peeled. Once she had started noticing the adverts, she could not stop, and their effect began to weaken.

Noor's younger brother Sami called round and complained, with a weary laugh, that his small daughter Yara begged for the cereal with the cartoon tiger on the box at every visit to the shop. Idris explained that children are especially open to such persuasion, since cartoon characters, bright colours and free toys speak directly to them. It was no sign of poor parenting, he said, merely proof that the people designing the box knew their business.

At the lunch, Noor took a small first plate and ate it slowly, praised the stew until her aunt blushed, and helped herself to a second portion of the vegetables with real pleasure. She went home carrying a box of leftovers and a heart full of warmth, and Auntie Leila waved from the doorway as though she had won a prize. It was the best meal Noor had eaten in weeks, and she had not once felt that she was on a diet.

Sami brought little Yara round for tea, and she pushed the broccoli to the very edge of her plate, as she had done at every meal for a month. Idris reassured him that this is perfectly ordinary, because children often need to try a new food many times, sometimes ten or more, before they come to like it. A refusal, he said, is not the end of the conversation but the beginning.

Idris suggested offering a very small piece, again and again, without any pressure, bribes or bargaining, because a child who feels forced often learns to dislike the food more. Children also learn a great deal by watching the people around them, so it helps enormously if the grown-ups at the table are seen enjoying the same dish. The method is slow, he admitted, but it is gentle, and it tends to work.

Noor admitted that she had loathed boiled cabbage as a child, and that she still crossed the room to avoid it. Idris smiled and told her that the tastes of adults change as well, since taste is shaped by experience, by cooking and by what we are used to eating. Nothing about it, he said, is carved in stone, and even a lifelong dislike can soften.

Many people report that after cutting down on sugar for a few weeks, sweet things begin to taste sweeter and some of their old favourites become almost too sweet to finish. Noor tested this on her tea, reducing the sugar a little each week, and by the end of the month she found her old cup undrinkable. The effect varies from person to person, Idris warned, but it was one of the nicer surprises in the whole business.

Salt behaves in a similar way, Idris said, for our liking for it adapts over a period of weeks, so that food which once seemed bland begins to taste properly seasoned. Herbs, spices, garlic and a squeeze of lemon can fill the gap while the tongue becomes accustomed to less, and many people end up enjoying their cooking more rather than less. He added that anyone who has a medical reason to watch their salt should follow their doctor's advice.

Idris insisted that healthy food must taste good, or nobody would go on eating it, and to prove his point he roasted a tray of carrots and cauliflower with a little oil and a spoonful of cumin. The edges turned brown and sweet, the kitchen filled with a warm, nutty smell, and Noor, who had always thought of vegetables as a duty, asked for a second helping. Roasting, he said, is the secret weapon of every cook who has ever persuaded a child.

For bitter greens, Idris had a handful of tricks, and he explained them with the air of a magician revealing his secrets. A pinch of salt, a drizzle of olive oil, a squeeze of lemon or a spell in a hot oven can all soften the bitterness, and none of them requires any particular skill. Noor, who had cheerfully avoided green leaves for years, discovered that she did not hate them at all, but had simply never been properly introduced.

Idris reminded her of a principle that had run through all his years of practice: adding a good thing is easier, and kinder, than banning a loved one. Noor began by stirring a handful of spinach into her morning eggs and a spoonful of grated carrot into her pasta sauce, and she hardly noticed the difference in taste. There was no sense of loss, only a slight feeling that her meals had quietly become better.

Noor and Hana decided to try one new food every week, and they kept a list on the office noticeboard with a column for love and a column for never again. Some weeks brought a delightful discovery and others brought a face of deep suspicion, but both kinds of result taught them something about their own tastes. The whole experiment cost almost nothing and gave them a delicious reason to talk to each other at lunch.

After about nine attempts, spread over a month, Yara picked up a small piece of broccoli on her fork and ate it without any fuss whatever. Sami remembered Idris's advice and said nothing at all, though he privately wanted to dance round the kitchen, and he merely smiled at his own plate. Noor, hearing the story that evening, felt that something in the whole business had been proved, even if it was only the value of patience.

Idris asked Noor to draw a timeline of her eating on an ordinary working day, and the shape that appeared surprised them both. She skipped breakfast, ate a small and rather sad lunch, and then arrived home so hungry that the evening became a long and ragged feast. Her appetite, it seemed, had been postponed all day and was now arriving with interest.

For many people, Idris explained, skipping meals leads straight to an overwhelming appetite later in the day, when willpower is lowest and the food is closest. A filling breakfast and regular meals can keep the evening hunger within bounds, although he was careful to add that people differ and that some manage perfectly well with a later first meal. The test was whether the evening felt calm or stormy, and for Noor it was plainly the latter.

Noor drew up a list of breakfasts that she actually liked and could make in ten minutes or less, since a plan that depends on an hour of cooking at dawn is no plan at all. Porridge, boiled eggs, yoghurt with fruit and wholemeal toast with beans all made the list, and each of them carried enough protein or fibre to keep her going until lunch. She stuck it inside the cupboard door, right next to the menu of comforts, where she could see it every morning.

Lunch, Noor decided, would no longer be a small and joyless salad eaten out of duty at her desk. She carried a box of last night's lentil stew to work, heated it in the office microwave and enjoyed a proper meal, with enough protein and fibre to see her through the long afternoon. Hana looked at it with envy and asked for the recipe before the box was empty.

Idris suggested that Noor plan a small snack for the late afternoon, since her notebook showed that the hunger which wrecked her evenings began at about four. A piece of fruit with a handful of nuts, or a small pot of yoghurt, would take the edge off without spoiling dinner, and it would stop the hunger from building into a storm. A snack eaten on purpose, he said, is quite different from a snack eaten in panic.

Eating more slowly, Idris reminded her, gives the fullness signals time to arrive before the plate is empty, and the simplest way to slow down is to put the fork down between mouthfuls. Noor tried to make each meal last about as long as a cup of tea, and she found that she often felt satisfied before she had finished everything on her plate. He called this a happy accident, although it was really the whole point of the exercise.

Idris handed her a single raisin and asked her to eat it as slowly as she possibly could, noticing its smell, its wrinkles, its texture and finally its taste. It felt faintly ridiculous at first, but Noor found that a raisin examined with real attention was a far larger experience than a handful swallowed in passing. The exercise was not meant for every meal, he said, only to show her what attention could do.

Idris mentioned that, for some people, thirst can be mistaken for hunger, although the evidence for this is modest and it does not apply to everyone. A glass of water costs nothing and takes a minute, he said, and if Noor was still hungry afterwards she should simply eat, without any argument or guilt. The aim was to understand her signals better and not to talk herself out of them.

Idris added, in the same unhurried tone, that alcohol can lower our caution and often goes hand in hand with salty snacks in the evening. It is not forbidden, and a glass of wine on a Saturday is hardly a crisis, but it is worth noticing in the notebook when it seems to feed the evening's appetite. Awareness, he repeated, was always the first step, and it needed no courage and no willpower at all.

Noor's new rhythm consisted of breakfast, lunch, a planned snack and dinner, and the late-night hunger that had once ruled her evenings arrived much less often. Idris stressed that daily rhythms differ from person to person, especially for night workers or for people who fast for their faith, and that the principle is simply to plan and to look after the hungry hours. The rhythm, in short, was a skeleton, and she was free to put flesh on it.

Planning a few easy dinners at the start of the week, Idris said, removes dozens of small and tiring decisions from the days ahead. On Sunday afternoon Noor wrote five simple dinners on a planner and stuck it to the fridge, leaving two evenings free for whatever life might bring. By Monday evening she realised that she had not had to ask herself what to eat, and the question had been a bigger burden than she knew.

Noor turned the planner into a shopping list, and Idris taught her the pleasant trick of choosing meals that share ingredients. A single bag of spinach, a tin of tomatoes and a pack of eggs might serve in three different dinners, so the shopping was shorter, the bill was smaller and nothing was left to wilt in the fridge. She began to feel faintly like the manager of a very small and efficient restaurant.

Every plan needs a rescue plan, Idris said, and he helped Noor to stock an emergency dinner kit for the evenings when everything else fell apart. Eggs, tinned beans, pasta, a bag of frozen vegetables and a jar of tomato sauce could be turned into a decent meal in fifteen minutes, with almost no thought. Knowing that it was there made the bad evenings feel far less like disasters.

Treats, Idris repeated, were not forbidden, and a life without them would be a poorer one. They are, however, better enjoyed slowly and on purpose than eaten in a rush at the end of a bad day, and Noor set out a single square of good dark chocolate on a small plate beside a candle. It tasted, to her great astonishment, like a small and private event, and she did not want it to end.

Idris offered a few tips for enjoying a treat to the full: sit down rather than eating on the move, give it your whole attention, begin with the best part and stop when it feels like enough. The first bites of any food are the most vivid, he explained, and the pleasure fades with each mouthful, so a smaller portion eaten with care can easily beat a larger one eaten without noticing. Noor tried it with a slice of lemon cake and was amazed at how long the delight lasted.

Eating out, Idris said, is a normal and happy part of life, and he had no wish to see Noor avoid restaurants for the sake of a plan. She could read the menu in advance, share a dish with a friend or take half of her meal home, and then settle down to enjoy the company and the conversation. A meal with friends, he reminded her, feeds a great deal more than the stomach alone.

Holidays, weddings and busy weeks will interrupt any plan, Idris warned, and nobody should feel they have failed when that happens. Noor travelled for a week to Hana's family wedding, where the food was wonderful and unending, and she ate freely, danced until midnight and refused to feel guilty about any of it. She came home pleasantly tired and with a bag of sweets for Idris, who accepted them gravely.

A week later Noor caught a heavy cold and had no energy for chopping, stirring or planning anything. She allowed the plan to pause and lived for three days on soup, toast and tea, because illness is a time for rest and not for rules. Idris added that anyone whose illness affects their eating for a long time, or who loses weight without meaning to, should speak to a doctor.

After the wedding and the cold, Noor's fridge was almost empty and her habits felt as rusty as an old bicycle. She did not try to restart the whole programme at once; she planned a single good meal, bought what she needed for it and cooked it that evening. The next one, she found, was easier, and by midweek the planner was back on the fridge door as though it had never left.

Idris and Noor sat down with the green notebook and went through the weeks together, sorting what truly worked from what merely looked good on paper. Some habits, such as the park bench and the planner, were obvious keepers, while others, such as the early morning gym, quietly slipped away without any drama. The plan was meant to fit her life, he said, and not the other way round, and a good plan bends instead of breaking.

Hana started a fashionable diet that she had found online, with strict rules about when to eat and what to leave out, and she was delighted with it for the first fortnight. Noor, watching her friend glow with enthusiasm, wondered whether she ought to copy her and abandon her own slow, careful plan. It was a fair question, and Idris treated it as one, with a long and thoughtful pause.

Idris explained that bodies differ in many ways, through their genes, their age, their sleep, their medicines, their histories and even the communities of microbes living in the gut. Studies have shown that different people can respond quite differently to exactly the same meal, in how full they feel and in how their blood sugar behaves. Science is only beginning to understand why, and Idris was happy to say so.

It follows, Idris said, that what works for a friend may not work for you, and that the cleverest diet in the world is useless if it does not suit your body and your life. Noor's notebook, with its patient record of times, moods and meals, was exactly the right instrument for discovering what worked for her. She had been an experimenter for weeks without knowing it, and the findings were hers alone.

Idris offered her four questions to ask about any new food claim that crossed her screen, whether from a friend, a magazine or a very cheerful stranger. Who benefits if I believe this, what is the evidence, is it extreme, and could I keep it up for years rather than days? Most fashionable diets, he said, fail on the fourth question long before they reach the first.

The best plan, Idris concluded, is usually the one that a person can actually keep, because a perfect diet that lasts a fortnight does less good than a decent one that lasts for years. Many different ways of eating can be healthy, according to the research, provided that they suit the person and include plenty of whole foods. Noor found this both reassuring and strangely freeing, as though a window had been opened in a stuffy room.

Eating good food matters for health in itself, Idris emphasised, whatever the number on the bathroom scale happens to say that morning. Noor decided to pay attention to her habits, her energy and her mood instead, and she put the scale in the back of a cupboard, behind the roasting tin. If she ever wanted to know about her weight, he added, a doctor would be the right person to ask.

Movement, Idris said, is good for the heart, the mind and the mood, but it should never be treated as a punishment for what one has eaten, since that turns a pleasure into a penalty. Noor and Hana turned their afternoon stroll into a Saturday morning walk along the river path, purely because they liked it and the light was beautiful. Nobody counted anything at all, and they came home hungry for an excellent breakfast.

Shame, Idris said, is a poor teacher, for it tends to backfire by sending people back to the very comfort they are ashamed of, while kindness towards oneself supports lasting change. Studies suggest that people who treat themselves gently after a slip tend to recover more quickly than those who punish themselves, though kindness is not a trick and cannot be faked. Noor thought of the green notebook and of her three underlined words, I was kind.

Idris reminded her that the bodies and meals on social media are carefully chosen, edited and lit, and that comparing ourselves with them is like measuring a cottage against a film set. Noor muted the accounts that made her feel small and followed instead a handful of cooks who simply loved their food, and her mood on the way to work improved at once. Her body, she thought, had never been the problem, and for the first time in years she believed it.

One quiet evening Noor wrote a short note to the woman she had been on that first night at the open fridge, the one who had suspected a flaw in her own character. She told her that she had never been weak, that she had merely not known how appetite works, and that none of it had ever been her fault. She folded the note, tucked it into the back of the green notebook and felt a weight she had carried for years lift quietly away.

Idris turned to a more serious subject, and he spoke more gently than ever. If eating feels out of control, if it has become extremely restricted, or if thoughts about food bring constant worry and distress, then this is a health matter and not a failure of willpower, and a doctor can help. Asking for that help, he added, is one of the strongest things a person can do.

Idris wanted to be certain that nobody mistook his stories for personal advice, because some people need guidance made especially for them. Those with medical conditions or allergies, anyone who is pregnant, and any parent worried about a child's eating should speak to a doctor or a registered dietitian rather than rely on general principles. A good professional, he said, fits the advice to the person, which is exactly what a book never can.

Idris smiled and confessed that in the first year of his retirement, when the clinic no longer filled his days, he had developed a small habit of eating chocolate at midnight. Even a dietitian with forty years of experience, he said, is subject to cues, tiredness and old appetite, and it had taken him a loop, a card and a new bedtime to change it. Noor laughed with enormous relief, and he laughed with her until the tea went cold.

Noor laid the first week of her notebook beside the most recent one and studied the two sets of pages with care. The late-night entries had dwindled from most nights to one or two a week, and the tone of the writing had changed even more than the numbers, from anxious and ashamed to curious and almost cheerful. She had not been cured of anything, because nothing had been wrong, but something had undoubtedly shifted.

On a card pinned beside the fridge, Noor listed the small changes that had made the most difference: a plan for the week, fruit in view, satisfying meals, enough sleep, and a kinder voice for her own mistakes. None of them was dramatic, and none required heroic willpower, but together they had quietly transformed the shape of her evenings. The old craving still came now and then, yet it no longer felt like an enemy.

Sami brought Yara to visit one afternoon, and Noor showed the little girl how to toss carrots in oil and spice before they went into the oven. Yara watched through the oven door as if it were a television, and then ate them hot from the tray, burning her fingers and demanding more. Nobody gave a single lecture, and the lesson, Noor reflected, was passed on exactly as it should be.

After a month Hana grew tired of her fashionable diet and its endless rules, and she asked Noor, rather sheepishly, how she had managed to change her evenings. Noor gave her a small notebook and a pencil, exactly as Idris had once given them to her, and explained that the first task was simply to be curious. Hana held the notebook for a moment as though it were something fragile and precious.

Twelve weeks after that first night, Noor stood at the open fridge at ten o'clock, lit by its cold glow, and felt the familiar craving rise. This time she recognised it at once, named it as tiredness, remembered that it was a wave and not a command, and put the kettle on. She ate one biscuit with her tea, slowly and without guilt, and went to bed feeling entirely like herself.

Standing at the window while Noor cooked, Idris summed up everything they had learned together over the months. Eating well is hard, he said, because a very old appetite now lives in a very modern food world, and it grows easier when you understand your body, shape your surroundings and speak to yourself with kindness. Small steps repeated with patience, in his long experience, almost always beat one heroic effort followed by a collapse.

Noor and Idris sat side by side at the kitchen table as the evening light faded, with two cups of tea and, in the middle, a small plate with one biscuit. This book has offered only general information about why healthy eating feels so hard, and the science is still growing, so it is not medical advice and cannot take the place of a doctor or a dietitian who knows you. If you are worried about your own eating, your health or your needs, please speak to a professional, and then be as kind to yourself as you would be to a friend.
